articles.title: Militant Buildup in Areas Critical to China’s Economic Interests in Pakistan
articles.full_text:
The TTP has stepped up its presence along the Karakoram Highway, even as Pakistan and China discuss $1.8 billion in financing to realign its Thakot-Raikot section.
Aerial view of the Karakoram Highway in Pakistan as seen in 2021.
With the China Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), a critical node of the Belt and Road Initiative in Pakistan, entering its second phase, insurgent and terrorist networks in Pakistan are strategically positioning themselves in areas critical to CPEC’s future.
CPEC connects China’s western Xinjiang province with the Arabian Sea. It enters Pakistan from the northern Gilgit-Baltistan area and culminates at Gwadar Port in Balochistan province.
While the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) is gradually increasing its footprint in Pakistan’s northern belt, the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) has ramped up attacks in Balochistan, multiplying China’s security challenges.
The deteriorating security situation in southwestern Balochistan and northern Pakistan is expected to disrupt future CPEC projects and China-Pakistan economic cooperation, thereby weakening Pakistan’s economy. The timing of militant buildup in these areas is vital; it is happening against the backdrop of intense U.S.-China competition over critical minerals in Balochistan.
Currently, China and Pakistan are discussing $1.8 billion in financing for the realignment of the Karakoram Highway’s (KKH) Thakot-Raikot section. In May 2028, when Diamer-Bhasha Dam becomes operational, a 280-kilometer section of KKH will be submerged in water. China has been delaying financing these projects for economic and security reasons. Concurrently, TTP has been increasing its presence in the area along the KKH.
It is important to mention that in July 2021 and March 2024, two unclaimed suicide attacks targeting buses carrying Chinese nationals working on the Dasu Hydropower Project took place along the KKH. Though no terrorist group officially claimed these attacks, individuals and militant networks involved in these attacks had past affiliations with TTP.
In December 2025, while disclosing its organizational restructuring, TTP announced a separate Wilayat (shadow province) for Kashmir, even as it split its Wilayat Gilgit Baltistan into two: Wilayat Diamer and Wilayat Darel. Then, in April 2026, TTP claimed responsibility for attacking police in Gilgit Baltistan’s Chilas area.
Concurrently, TTP’s network has re-emerged in Malakand Division, which abuts Gilgit Baltistan. On August 2, TTP claimed a suicide attack outside a police station in Swat, which killed 17 people and wounded dozens of others. Together, Gilgit Baltistan and Malakand Division are critical for CPEC’s future.
Critically, the recent U.N. Monitoring Committee on Al-Qaeda and ISIL report indicates reconcentration of the East Turkistan Islamic Movement (ETIM)’s fighters in northern Afghanistan’s Badakhshan province, which shares a border with Gilgit Baltistan. The near-simultaneous moves by TTP and ETIM to increase their footprints in Gilgit Baltistan, Malakand Division and Badakhshan, respectively, are not coincidental. These are synchronized moves by these militant groups to strategically position themselves in areas vital to China’s future economic interests.
Separately, in July 2026, Jamaat-ul-Ahrar (JuA) broke away from TTP and is now working independently. The exit frees JUA from TTP’s code of conduct and organizational discipline to freelance.
In the past, JuA has carried out attacks in Pakistan on behalf of the Islamic State of Khorasan Province (ISKP).
In 2014, JuA’s Omar Khalid Khorasani wanted to become the emir of the Islamic State’s Wilayat Khorasan. However, the Islamic State turned down his demand and appointed Hafiz Saeed Khan Orakzai as the first emir, hence ending their short-lived partnership.
In the past, JuA has threatened China’s economic interests in Pakistan. In 2014, the 9th issue of JuA’s propaganda magazine Ihya-e-Khilafat ran an article titled “The Hidden Motives Behind the Chinese Investment in Pakistan,” written by its then spokesperson Ehsanullah Ehsan.
On its part, ISKP is the most vocal anti-China terrorist group in the Afghanistan-Pakistan region. It has attacked Chinese nationals and interests in Quetta, Kabul, Kunar, Takhar, Nuristan and Badakhshan. Keeping in view their overlapping anti-China postures, ISKP could once again outsource its anti-China campaign to JuA.
In Balochistan, the southwestern stretch of Pakistan, BLA has been hitting Chinese nationals and interests both vocally and physically since 2018. The recent spate of violence is strategically directed against Chinese economic interests. The alarming rise in BLA’s attacks in Chagai district has created security and logistical issues for Chinese state-owned Metallurgical Corporation of China (MCC), which is jointly mining gold and copper from the Saindak Copper and Gold Mine with Pakistan-owned Saindak Metals Limited since the early 2000s. Following the deteriorating security situation and hazardous road conditions in Chagai, especially on the N40 Highway, the MCC has written a letter to Pakistan’s Energy Ministry to ensure the sustainability of supply chains. Otherwise, it has warned that the mining operations could be halted.
Likewise, in April, BLA’s first-ever attack on a patrol boat of the Pakistan Coast Guard (PCG) in the Arabian Sea near Jiwani, and the Suicide Vehicle Borne Improvised Explosive Device (SVBIED) assault targeting a PCG check post in the same area in July point to new operational capabilities. After attacking the PCG boat, BLA formally announced its naval unit, the Hammal Maritime Defense Force.
The terror group has also used weaponized Chinese commercial drones for attacks in Gwadar. Together, the uptick of violence and new operational capabilities in Chagai and Gwadar, where strategic mines and Gwadar Port are located, ostensibly underline a new phase of the Baloch militants’ anti-China campaign in Balochistan.
Pakistan will have to revamp its internal security framework to ensure security of Chinese projects and nationals in the country. Intelligence coordination among various security institutions, a robust understanding of terrorist networks in areas like Gilgit Baltistan, Malakand, Chagai and Gwadar, will help them devise tailored security frameworks to deter such attacks. At the same time, paying attention to genuine local grievances through a participatory development approach and giving local communities stakes in upcoming CPEC projects will also act as an extra layer of security for China and Pakistan. Increasing the stakes and involvement of local communities in these projects will undermine the ability of terrorist groups to exploit their grievances and recruit them for attacks.

articles.title: One Nation’s Dual Assault on Australia’s Structural Realities
articles.full_text:
With a below replacement-level birth rate and a booming elder population, One Nation’s anti-immigration stance, combined with its critique of superannuation, is a toxic combo.
A major structural issue facing most Western and East Asian countries at present is their below replacement-level birth rates. This has the potential to create an unfavorable dependency ratio – the problem of aging societies with a large cohort of retirees, but not enough workers to pay for pensions, healthcare, and other essential services. 
Yet simultaneously, many Western countries are experiencing an insurgence of populist, and often extremist, parties hostile to the one mechanism available to alleviate this problem: immigration. In Australia, this year has seen the rise of One Nation – previously a small fringe anti-immigrant party – now consistently polling in the mid-high 20 percent range. One Nation often matches the governing Labor Party’s poll numbers, and is polling far ahead of Australia’s other traditional major political force, the permanent coalition between the Liberal and National parties. 
One Nation’s reason for existence is to undermine Australia’s migration program – which it sees as a threat to their idea of the Australian nation. Yet as the party has ascended in the polls it has needed to branch out into other populist causes and conspiratorial theories to promote. One issue the party has landed on is Australia’s retirement savings scheme – known as superannuation. 
Australia’s superannuation scheme was made compulsory in its modern form by the Keating government in 1992, requiring employers to contribute a portion of workers’ wages into privately managed retirement funds. The contribution rate has gradually risen to 12 percent – paid on top of wages – and has created one of the world’s largest pools of retirement savings. It is accessible at 60 years old. The basic idea is simple: Australians build up their own nest egg during their working lives, reducing their reliance on the government-funded Age Pension in retirement. Superannuation is ranked one of the world’s leading retirement schemes.  
However, there’s always been a strain of suspicion toward superannuation within the Liberal Party. This stems in part from politics – the scheme was introduced by the Labor Party, after all – and in part from the perception of the scheme as paternalistic and undermining the personal responsibility to save for yourself. 
But within a consumerist culture, turbo-charged by the ease of online shopping and the relentless product promotion of online influencers, it is arguable that the scheme has saved a great many Australians from difficult retirements. articles.title: Tokayev Sets Agenda for Kazakhstan as New Parliament Gets to Work
articles.full_text:
The change in form promised by Kazakhstan’s new parliament does not appear to be matched by a change in its function.
Kazakhstan’s new unicameral parliament, the Kurultai, gathered for its first session today. On August 23 the all-but-ordained Adilet party triumphed over an array of officially sanctioned opposition parties, winning a thumping 71 percent of the vote in the first election after Kazakhstan’s March constitutional revamp.
According to the Central Electoral Commission, which registered new legislators in an official ceremony on August 27, Adilet will have 110 deputies of a possible 145 sitting in the new body, likely led by presidential advisor-turned-party leader Aibek Dadebay. 
As for its legislative agenda, all signs indicate that the Kurultai will largely pick up where the old parliament left off. Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev spent the last week plotting a roadmap for the incoming Kurultai, and his to-do list is grounded in long-standing governmental priorities. 
On August 27, for example, citing the example of “several well-developed countries,” Tokayev said he planned to ask Kurultai deputies to consider banning social media for children under the age of 16, in what will essentially be a continuation of a bill submitted to parliament in June, according to local independent media outlet Vlast.kz. 
In a similar vein, speaking at an educators’ conference on August 26, Tokayev called on the government to take more urgent measures to implement his May presidential decree on the introduction of artificial intelligence into the national education system. The directive came as part of the country’s Year of Artificial Intelligence program, itself a continuation of the broader strategy on AI launched in 2025 following the creation of the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development. 
Amid these more conventional proposals, Tokayev’s most interesting comments arguably came during  an appearance at a polling station on August 23 — and not only because he rebuked his compatriots for hugging and kissing in contravention of the country’s “time-honored traditions,” and called on Kazakhstani men to instead shake hands “firmly,” not like a “warm cutlet or a twig.” 
Speaking after casting his ballot, Tokayev also suggested that Kazakhstan needed to be “turned into a major building site,” and proposed transferring significant amounts of money from the National Fund to spur this drive for development, a policy hastily confirmed by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin at a briefing on August 25. 
According to Zhumangarin, Kazakhstan’s government is set to withdraw nearly 12 trillion tenge ($26.2 billion) from the National Fund, the country’s sovereign wealth fund, despite pledging last summer to scale down transfers through 2028 to reduce the national budget’s dependence on oil revenues. (Kazakhstan’s National Fund is largely financed by revenues generated from the country’s oil and other extractive industries, with a portion of these revenues saved and invested for future generations.)
This too, however, equates to picking up where previous governments left off. As Kazakhstani political scientist Daniyar Ashimbayev wrote, “the National Fund has for years been actively misappropriated for unclear purposes,” with the state dipping into the reserve to inject money into the economy, “without concerning itself with the wisdom of such spending.” 
What this all means is that the change in form promised by Kazakhstan’s new parliament does not appear to be matched by a change in its function. The Kurultai may have a number of new politicians taking their seats today, but the policies, practices, and priorities shaping the country’s politics remain largely unchanged.

articles.title: Domestic Politics Is Making an India Visit Difficult for Bangladeshi PM Tarique Rahman
articles.full_text:
The Jamaat-e-Islami and the National Citizen Party are objecting to Rahman visiting Delhi.
India’s Minister for External Affairs S. Jaishankar hands over a letter of condolence from Prime Minister Narendra Modi to Tarique Rahman, then the acting chairman of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party, following the death of his mother and former Bangladesh Prime Minister Begum Khaleda Zia, on Jaishankar’s arrival at Dhaka for Zia’s funeral, Dec. 31, 2025.
A visit to India by Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is long overdue. Bangladeshi prime ministers have traditionally made India the destination of their first visit after coming to power. But over six months after Rahman’s inauguration, the much-anticipated visit is yet to happen. Meanwhile, the Bangladeshi PM has visited Malaysia and China.
Delhi has invited Rahman to India for a bilateral visit as well as to participate in the upcoming BRICS summit that it is hosting in September. Rahman’s visit was initially seen in Bangladesh as a chance for Dhaka and New Delhi to reset relations that deteriorated after the ouster of the Sheikh Hasina government on August 5, 2024.
However, the visit seems unlikely to happen. Indeed, it has brought Bangladesh’s domestic politics into the equation, with moves by the Rahman government to improve relations with New Delhi now risking criticism at home.
Over the past several weeks, officials from both countries have been discussing a bilateral visit. According to a media report in mid-August that cited Bangladeshi diplomatic sources, the two sides were discussing dates for a possible visit. It was expected to happen between August 20 and 25. Preparations for the visit went pretty far. On August 21, the Indian President’s Office briefly issued a notice saying its Change of Guard ceremony would be cancelled because of a rehearsal for the ceremonial welcome of the Bangladeshi prime minister. However, the notice was withdrawn within an hour.
It seems that Rahman’s visit will not happen.
One of the main obstacles is Sheikh Hasina, who has been in India since she fled after her government was toppled. In November 2025, Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal convicted her of crimes against humanity over the deadly crackdown on the 2024 uprising, and sentenced her to death in absentia. Dhaka has since formally asked India to extradite her so the verdict can be enforced.
On August 5 this year, the second anniversary of Hasina’s ouster from power, the former prime minister addressed an online media interaction in New Delhi. When the Bangladeshi government objected, India said a private media body was organizing the event and that the government neither organized it nor endorsed Hasina’s remarks. But in Bangladesh, India’s explanation did little to calm the criticism.
Bangladesh’s Foreign Ministry said the media event was damaging efforts to improve bilateral relations. Dhaka had already asked India not to allow Hasina or other Awami League (AL) figures to use Indian territory for political activities directed at Bangladesh.
The National Citizen Party (NCP) took the hardest position. Its leaders demanded that the Indian high commissioner in Dhaka be summoned. NCP convener Nahid Islam stressed that Rahman should not visit India before it returned Hasina and others wanted by Bangladesh. NCP spokesperson Asif Mahmud said that Rahman’s visit to Delhi would be a betrayal of the people.
Rahman has strong reasons to repair relations with India. India surrounds Bangladesh on three sides. It is an important trade and transit partner. Water, border management, energy, connectivity, and security require regular cooperation.
But the political environment inside Bangladesh has changed sharply since 2024.
For years, one of the main criticisms that Bangladeshis levelled against India was the excessive influence it wielded over Bangladesh through its close relationship with Hasina and the Awami League. New Delhi may see it differently, but this is a widely held view in Bangladeshi political circles, especially post-2024. Hasina’s continued stay in India has made it harder to separate that past from the present.
That is why Hasina’s political activity from India is such a sensitive issue for Bangladeshis. For many Bangladeshis, the issue is not only whether New Delhi supports her, but why she is still allowed to speak and act politically from India, while Bangladesh is seeking her extradition.
The government has also hardened its language. On August 16, the Foreign Ministry said a “propitious environment” was needed before Rahman could visit India. It linked the prime ministerial visit to the extradition of Hasina and other fugitives. On August 21, Rahman’s press secretary said that no decision had been made on the prime minister’s India visit and that Dhaka was waiting for India’s response.
However, the opposition is not united on what Rahman should do.
Jamaat-e-Islami (JI), Bangladesh’s largest Islamist party, strongly criticized Hasina’s online appearance at the Delhi media event. JI Secretary General Miya Ghulam Parwar called it a gross violation of diplomatic norms. However, JI chief and Leader of the Opposition Shafiqur Rahman later said the prime minister could visit India. His condition was that bilateral relations must be based on equality, mutual respect, and friendship, not Indian hegemony.
Although it is part of the JI-led coalition, the NCP struck a harder line. While JI used strong nationalist language, it did not reject engagement with India itself. The NCP, however, has tried to stop or delay the visit until specific demands were met.
The visit of Parag Jain, chief of the Research and Analysis Wing (India’s external intelligence agency), to Dhaka on August 9, when he met Bangladeshi security officials, has further complicated matters. Bangladeshi authorities described the trip as routine and said it took place at the invitation of Bangladesh’s Directorate General of Forces Intelligence (DGFI), with the government rejecting claims that the visit was secret. However, the timing of Jain’s visit, ahead of a planned visit by Rahman to Delhi, made it a sensitive one. Intelligence engagement with India revived memories of the Hasina years and strengthened allegations that India was exerting pressure on Dhaka.
There is little evidence that a coordinated anti-India bloc deliberately derailed Rahman’s visit. But the political reaction has clearly made a visit to Delhi more difficult for Rahman.
Rahman cannot afford to look weak before India. India, meanwhile, is unlikely to accept that Hasina’s extradition must be resolved before high-level engagement. New Delhi says the request is being examined through established procedures.
So, while domestic politics is influencing how the Rahman government approaches efforts to improve relations with India, Delhi wants to rebuild ties, but its continued hosting of Hasina has become the biggest obstacle to that effort.
The Delhi visit may still happen as both sides continue to talk on the matter. But whenever Rahman eventually goes, his challenge will be to improve ties with India without making Bangladeshis feel that the Hasina-era relationship is coming back.
Meanwhile, the Rahman government is facing multiple problems at home. Law and order is deteriorating. The energy crisis is affecting both people and businesses. Factories have been forced to halt or cut production. Creating enough jobs, especially for young people, is another challenge.
The government therefore has little room for maneuver. Cooperation with India is needed to improve the economic situation in Bangladesh. But if tensions over India lead to wider unrest at home, it will put the government under additional stress. That is something Rahman would like to avoid – at least for now.
There may, however, be an easier way for Rahman to engage with India. The BRICS summit on September 12–13 could offer an opening. As BIMSTEC chair, India has invited Rahman to attend its outreach session. Dhaka has not confirmed his participation so far. Politically, that may be easier than a bilateral visit, as he would be travelling for a multilateral summit rather than solely for talks with India.

However, the visit seems unlikely to happen. Indeed, it has brought Bangladesh’s domestic politics into the equation, with moves by the Rahman government to improve relations with New Delhi now risking criticism at home.

articles.title: China’s Green Exports to Europe Are a Bright Spot Amid Trade Tensions
articles.full_text:
Climate change and the Iran war are driving many European consumers to Chinese-made electric vehicles despite EU tariffs.
A BYD Atto 3 charges on the street in Berlin, Germany, Sep. 24, 2023.
China’s economy showed further signs of stagnation in July, according to delayed figures released from China’s National Bureau of Statistics on August 17. But one economic bright spot China’s government could point to was sales of Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) to western Europeans. 
According to data gathered by Schmidt Automotive Research over the first five months of 2026, sales of Chinese EV models in western Europe rose to 14.2 percent of total EVs sold between January and May. This means around one in seven EVs sold in the region were Chinese-made, despite significant EU tariffs on Chinese EV exports since 2024. Such tariffs are not replicated in the United Kingdom, accounting for some, but not all, of the recent surge in Chinese EV sales in many western European markets. 
Despite growing trade tensions between the EU and China, the uptick in sales is being driven by consumer responses to two factors: conflict and climate change.
Europe is having a record-breaking heatwave this summer. Soaring temperatures have brought drought, wildfires, and higher electricity bills for households and businesses as European demand for air conditioning rises. The rise in natural disasters and other fallout from climate change is causing mounting insurance costs and business losses across the continent. These changes are accelerating Europe’s move toward a greener economy as more households and firms buy heat pumps, solar panels and EVs to decarbonize their activities. 
Meanwhile, the on-again, off-again conflict between the United States and Iran since February has caused European petrol and diesel prices to surge. The fuel spikes have improved the attractiveness to European drivers of ditching fossil fuels and switching to a battery-powered vehicle less exposed to crude oil price swings.
Many Chinese EV manufacturers were quick to respond to an increase in Western European demand for their products this year, incentivized by a severe price war in their domestic market. Chinese manufacturers have exported over 120 EV designs to Europe this year compared to around 100 EV designs from European car companies. Chinese firms like BYD, Chery, SAIC, and Xpeng are expanding their Europe footprints despite tariffs and factors like the EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). This would introduce “Made in Europe” requirements in areas like public procurement. The IAA is one of several actual or proposed EU instruments China complains are aimed against its exporters to act as non-tariff trade barriers.
The EU is becoming more protectionist in part because it fears the long-term danger of over-reliance upon Chinese exports, including clean technology products: weaponized dependencies, cybersecurity risks, and espionage threats to the bloc. Some think tanks have even claimed China’s clean technology itself presents a national security threat for Europe. 
The United States will likely encourage European countries to take a wary view of Chinese smart and clean technology exports as more Chinese manufacturers try to expand their footprint there. U.S. lawmakers are already leading the way with the Connected Vehicle Security Act. This would ban imports of China-linked smart vehicles, including EVs, and components by 2030. The legislation would also block Chinese smart cars’ entry into the U.S. from Canada or Mexico. There is a low-probability, but high-impact scenario, that the EU could mimic this approach in areas like EVs.
While not engaged in a trade war with Beijing yet, Europe’s opposition to China’s current industrial development strategy is growing, as is its fear of becoming even more dependent upon Chinese technology and supply chains. China has used its dominance of critical mineral supply chains to severely constrain Japan’s access to these goods. It could use similar restrictions in the future to threaten Western defense supply chains. 
Beijing has increasingly used its economic and political leverage to demand concessions from foreign governments on matters like Taiwan, Tibet, or its maritime boundary disputes in the South China Sea. European governments increasingly fear similar Chinese actions against them in future diplomatic disputes. 
Already, European car manufacturers’ operations were disrupted last year when China restricted automotive chip supplies to Europe after the Dutch government tried to take over Nexperia. This global semiconductor company is a subsidiary of Chinese technology firm Wingtech, and Beijing reacted sharply to this perceived Dutch infringement on a Chinese asset. This confirmed Europe’s fear about its exposure to Chinese trade and technology pressures. 
Security concerns are intertwined with Europe’s frustration with its growing trade deficit with China. This reached a record 359.9 billion euros in 2025, with the EU arguing that the significant asymmetry in market openings between itself and China is at least partially to blame for this gap. Signs of continued Chinese penetration of European markets, such as higher EV sales, will likely mean another worsening of the bloc’s trade deficit with China in 2026.
In June, the EU set a three-month deadline to achieve “tangible” results from China regarding issues like the trade deficit or Chinese non-tariff trade barriers reducing EU firms’ market access there. EU Trade Commissioner Maroc Sefcovic will travel to Beijing in October to assess the progress the two sides have made. 
The EU is also considering fresh measures like tariffs on Chinese plug-in hybrid EVs, independent of the October trade talks. Meanwhile, China has signaled it intends to retaliate against any future EU trade restrictions, rather than make concessions. The conditions for a China-EU trade war are accumulating, even if one has not yet begun in 2026.
However, regardless of the destabilizing direction of relations on trade and other issues, the EU faces counterbalancing pressures to continue imports of Chinese clean technology products like EVs, solar panels, and wind turbines. EU policymakers will likely require access to China’s advanced EV and battery technologies to meet targets like achieving a 100 percent reduction in new vehicles’ emissions from 2035.
EU attempts to reindustrialize and shift to a green economy by 2050 will likewise likely require buy-in from Chinese manufacturers for Europe-based facilities, and injections of Chinese capital to help modernize the continent’s preexisting power and transport infrastructure. EU fears about China’s economic and geopolitical threats will need to be reconciled with its ambitions for domestic economic and technological transformation.
Ultimately, the EU seeks a sustainable accommodation with China rather than a conflict for supremacy, like the one that is increasingly shaping the China-U.S. relationship. China’s decision to put clean technologies and other so-called “new quality productive forces” at the heart of its quest for renewed economic growth means aggressive EU barriers to Chinese exports of these products would trigger a major confrontation that Beijing is probably better placed to weather. 
Equally, however, opinion in the EU and non-EU European states like the U.K. is a lot more skeptical of China today. There is increasing agreement among European governments – including long-time holdouts like Germany – about the need to toughen policy toward Beijing. The German government has examined ways to damage China economically in the event of a trade war, a major policy shift.
Chinese exporters are therefore likely to complain significantly of worsening treatment by European – and especially EU – governments, even as China continues to sell large amounts of EVs and other goods to European customers. The EU is expected to increase the number of investigations into Chinese green manufacturers for breaching fair trade rules on issues like state subsidies, which will anger Beijing. 
There is a strong chance that the two sides will engage in several bouts of trade warfare after October and moving into next year. Nevertheless, Chinese clean technology exports to Europe will likely remain a bright spot for bilateral trade, as external factors like climate change, price wars, or conflict incentivize both European consumers and Chinese exporters to continue the trade that is driving Europe’s switch from fossil fuel economies to the one envisaged in its European Green Deal.

U.S. lawmakers are already leading the way with the Connected Vehicle Security Act. This would ban imports of China-linked smart vehicles, including EVs, and components by 2030. The legislation would also block Chinese smart cars’ entry into the U.S. from Canada or Mexico. There is a low-probability, but high-impact scenario, that the EU could mimic this approach in areas like EVs.
articles.summary: Climate change and the Iran war are driving many European consumers to Chinese-made electric vehicles despite EU tariffs.

articles.title: Transitional Justice or Political Retaliation? Bangladesh’s Journalists on Trial
articles.full_text:
As Bangladesh’s tribunal for 1971 atrocities is being used to prosecute journalists, the line between accountability and revenge is being tested.
An estimated 1,400 people died in the July uprising of 2024, which led to Sheikh Hasina’s ouster on August 5, 2024. To contribute to accountability, reconciliation, and a sense of justice for the Bangladeshi people, the International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) was revived.
Created in 2010 based on the 1973 ICT act, the tribunal was designed to prosecute atrocities committed during the 1971 Liberation War. It was heavily criticized – especially in 2011-2012 but throughout her tenure – for being used by Hasina to put opposition figures on trial for 1971-era crimes. The ICT was seen as politically instrumentalized and lacking due process. 
This year, three journalists and a secular writer were arrested and accused before the ICT of crimes against humanity through incitement in connection with their reporting. They have been imprisoned for almost two years now on a wave of murder charges in the regular courts. Human rights organizations have condemned the murder charges and have raised concerns that the tribunal may now be used against figures associated with the former governing order, including journalists. 
“The crimes committed against the student-led movement in July and August 2024, in which hundreds were killed, demand a proper accounting, and those responsible should face justice,” said Toby Cadman, a human rights lawyer and former advisor to the ICT’s Chief Prosecutor. “The victims and the country are entitled to a process directed at truth, justice and reconciliation rather than retribution, and that makes it all the more important that these trials meet the highest standards of due process – properly particularized charges, timely disclosure, effective access to counsel, and meaningful judicial review of detention.” 
Four Bangladeshi journalists – Farzana Rupa, her husband Shakil Ahmed, Mozammel Babu, and Shyamal Dutta – and writer Shahriar Kabir have faced criminal proceedings connected to the uprising. All have been imprisoned since 2024. 
Rupa and Shakil were initially arrested at Dhaka airport on August 21, 2024, in connection with a murder case concerning the death of a garment worker named Fazlul. In the following months, they were produced before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate’s Court several times in connection with new cases. Rupa reportedly faces nine murder cases, while Shakil faces six. 
Mozammel Babu, Shyamal Dutta, and Shahriar Kabir were arrested in September 2024 under similar uprising-related murder charges. 
In a Daily Star interview published on November 21, 2024, Dr. Muhammad Yunus, then head of the interim government, acknowledged that the murder cases filed against journalists had been “done hastily” and distanced the government from the charges. 
His then law adviser, Asif Nazrul, went further at a press-freedom roundtable on June 26, 2025, disclosing that 266 journalists had been sued. He stressed that the cases “were not initiated by the government – they were filed by ordinary citizens,” adding, “[W]e have made it clear that no arrests should be made unless there is substantial evidence.”
The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), which came to power in February 2026, made its own explicit pledge in its election manifesto to ensure press freedom by reviewing the Digital Security Act, preventing attacks on media outlets, withdrawing politically motivated cases, and ensuring justice for tortured and murdered journalists. Yet neither commitment has translated into relief for the four journalists and one writer. 
Since their arrest in 2024, family members of those accused have filed numerous bail applications, citing lack of evidence, an absence of a prima facie case, and the advanced age or poor health of several defendants – Shahriar Kabir, aged 75, and Babu, who is suffering from cancer. Bail applications for Kabir and Babu have been continuously rejected. On May 11, 2026, the Dhaka High Court granted interim bail to Rupa in six cases and to Shakil in five. The Appellate Division subsequently suspended the bail granted to Rupa and Shakil.
Earlier this year, in a significant escalation, Rupa, Babu, Dutta, and Kabir were all arrested in separate ICT cases. The first case concerns Ekattor TV’s coverage and a subsequent documentary on the 2013 Shapla Chattar crackdown, implicating Rupa, Babu, and Kabir. A second ICT proceeding, initiated in August 2026 concerning the July uprising of 2024, named Rupa, Babu, and Dutta. At the second case’s hearing on August 25, 2026, they were arrested in that case as well. 
The journalists now face proceedings on two tracks. Ordinary criminal charges run through regular courts, where bail can be granted. The ICT proceedings are separate, governed by a distinct legal framework, and involve allegations of crimes against humanity. 
The uncertainty has taken a toll on the families of those detained. Rupa and Shakil’s daughter, Monphool, was only 17 when both of her parents were arrested. She has spent the past two years working for their release, abandoning her own education to advocate for them. 
Monphool described falling asleep and waking up each day “asking the same question – whether today will be the day my mother or father comes home.” She lives in a state of “constant fear that cannot be put down. Ordinary conversations, home-cooked meals together, birthdays, things that most families often take for granted, have been lost.” 
“Waiting, every single day, has changed me,” Monphool said. “Cases like my parents’ have become a pattern in Bangladesh for far too long and many other families have already experienced what I am going through. I feel like I have lost my childhood to something that I have no control over, I only hope that it will come to an end.” 
The ICT as Political Instrument: A Recurring Political Pattern 
Moving from multiple murder cases to charges of crimes against humanity is a significant escalation. Under the 1973 Act, crimes against humanity require acts committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack against a civilian population. Portraying a protest as “provocative,” producing a television documentary, or asking a prime minister a pointed question at a press conference during the July uprising does not fall within this ambit.
Crucially, Bangladesh’s law historically lacked the mandatory requirement to prove that an alleged crime was part of such a “widespread or systematic attack,” as Article 7 of the Rome Statute demands. International legal scholars, Human Rights Watch, and Amnesty International flagged this gap during the 2010–2011 proceedings, but the Bangladesh Supreme Court’s 2013 judgment in Abdul Quader Molla v. Government of Bangladesh (arising from ICT-BD Case No. 02 of 2012) declined to incorporate the threshold. 
That leaves the tribunal free to try crimes against humanity by domestic standards incompatible with international law. While the interim government moved to amend the ICT Ordinance to align statutory definitions with the Rome Statute, how these legal standards are executed in practice remains contested. 
Procedural weaknesses compound the problem. Interlocutory orders on arrest, detention, or bail cannot be appealed; the Constitution suspends fundamental protections, including the right to a speedy, public trial, for anyone charged under the Act. Because the Act sets no distinct sentencing thresholds, a documentary producer and a perpetrator of mass atrocities face the same maximum penalty: death. 
Defense lawyers, meanwhile, report receiving nothing in writing corroborating the allegations even after their clients are shown arrested, with months passing before a charge sheet – and a real defense – becomes possible. 
As Cadman put it, true justice requires “prosecutorial discipline.” That means, he explained, “Charges should be brought only where there is a strong evidential basis for them. A case brought without that foundation does not simply fail; it weakens the cases that deserve to succeed, and it invites the very skepticism the Tribunal can least afford.” 
The 1973 Act was built to prosecute the Pakistan Army and its collaborators for 1971 wartime atrocities. Stretching that machinery to reach a decade-old broadcast or a reporter’s question transforms a transitional justice mechanism into a tool for ordinary political disputes. 
Importantly, international jurisprudence has already dealt with the question of journalists and crimes against humanity. 
“On journalists specifically, international law is settled and it is demanding,” said Cadman. “The Rwanda tribunal’s media jurisprudence establishes that liability does not attach to reporting, commentary or editorial line, however partisan. RTLM’s broadcasters were convicted because they broadcast the names, addresses and vehicle registrations of identified individuals so that they could be hunted down and killed, while the killing was underway – and even on those facts the Appeals Chamber in Nahimana reversed a substantial part of the trial judgment, holding that hate speech falling short of a direct call to commit the crime is not incitement, and that seniority at a broadcaster is no substitute for proof of the accused’s own contribution, intent and knowledge.” 
Cadman concluded: “…[F]or crimes against humanity the speech must additionally form part of the widespread or systematic attack charged. That is the threshold. It should be applied in Bangladesh as it would be anywhere else.”
Justice, Not Vendetta – Toward a Principled Standard 
Bangladesh’s political transition presents an opportunity to break the cycle in which each ruling coalition criminalizes its predecessors. A durable democratic transition requires stable institutions whose rules apply uniformly, narrow evidence-based prosecutions of grave violations, and a clear distinction between perpetrators, political associates, and journalists.
articles.summary: As Bangladesh’s tribunal for 1971 atrocities is being used to prosecute journalists, the line between accountability and revenge is being tested.

articles.title: China’s Tourism Industry Gains Momentum Thanks to Visa-Free Policies
articles.full_text:
China is poised to become a global powerhouse as both a source and destination for international tourism.
In the first six months of 2026, China received 22.91 million visits from foreign nationals, up 20.4 percent year on year. The uptick is the result of China’s visa-free policy, which accounts for 77.7 percent of all foreign arrivals. 
Earlier this year, China announced that starting February 17, 2026 all ordinary passport holders from Canada and the United Kingdom can travel to its mainland for up to 30 days without a visa. The expansion in China’s unilateral visa-exemption program to include Canada and the U.K. followed recent visits to Beijing by leaders from the two countries as they seek to reset ties. According to China’s Foreign Ministry, the visa-free program – expected to run until December 31, 2026 – aims to foster people-to-people exchanges, the foundation for cross-cultural understanding, economic interdependence, and peaceful diplomatic relations. 
For the United Kingdom, which sees China as an important tourist destination as well as a source market, attempts to eliminate barriers to cross-border tourism are certainly a step in the right direction. Data from the U.K.’s Office for National Statistics showed that around 620,000 British people traveled to China in 2024. According to VisitBritain, the national tourism agency, in the same year, the U.K. welcomed 463,000 visitors from China (41 percent were holiday visits, in line with the market average), generating a total expenditure of 723.8 million pounds. In the coming years, a new report from VisitBritain estimates that China’s visitor market will be worth around £1.2 billion in terms of visitor spending in 2026. The agency forecast that tourism from China to the U.K. will expand rapidly, by 20 percent annually through 2030.
Similarly, as Canada seeks to reset relations with Beijing, the newly implemented visa-free policy is expected to further facilitate two-way travel. According to Canada’s Foreign Minister Anita Anand, the change is “making travel easier, supporting business exchanges, and strengthening people-to-people ties.’’ 
For China, the offer of visa-free travel for nationals of Canada and the U.K. is only part of a larger trend. As part of efforts to further open up and attract foreign visitors after the COVID-19 pandemic, on December 1, 2023 China  commenced the trial implementation of unilateral visa-free entry policies for ordinary passport holders from six countries: Germany, France, Malaysia, Spain, the Netherlands and Italy. Over the trial period, the expanded visa-free policy helped support China’s tourism industry growth. Beijing has thus continued with the approach, eventually expanding visa-free access to include 50 countries.
As the expanded visa-free program facilitated international travel, China experienced a record 697 million inbound and outbound crossings in 2025, according to data from the National Immigration Administration. That represented a 14.2 percent year-on-year increase. International visitors made more than 82 million crossings in 2025, marking a 26.4 percent increase compared to 2024, and over 73 percent of these travelers benefitted from China’s visa-free program. 
The inclusion of new members in China’s unilateral visa-free scheme – which now includes 35 countries from Europe, seven in Asia, six in the Americas, and two in Oceania – will not only enhance people-to-people exchanges but also support broader economic benefits. 
According to U.N. Tourism, China in 2023 recovered its position as the top spender on international tourism at $196.5 billion, followed by the United States ($150 billion), Germany ($112 billion), the U.K. ($110 billion), and France ($49 billion). The latest Economic Impact Research (EIR) data from the World Travel & Tourism Council showed more than 68 million international visitors entered China in 2025, up 15.5 percent year on year, nearly three times the global growth rate of 5.4 percent. At the same time, international visitor spending expanded by 10.5 percent to $135 billion, surpassing pre-pandemic levels and significantly outperforming the global average growth of 3.2 percent.
Ultimately, as China grows as a source market as well as a destination, the rise of the tourism industry is critical to both the Chinese economy and global tourism. The WTM Global Travel report estimated that from 2024 to 2033 the share of Chinese households with purchasing power to embark on international travel will roughly double. The growth of China’s middle class could add more than 60 million households to the count of those that can afford international travel. 
Interestingly, this figure represents just 2.3 percent of the country’s entire population, showing the Chinese market’s enormous potential for future growth. By 2033 the Chinese market, depending on its growth trajectory and other factors including connectivity, could be up to twice the size of the United States as a source market in terms of spending. 
Meanwhile, China is also forecast to be among the top five destination markets in terms of visitor spending (along with the United States, Spain, Thailand and Turkiye). 
Since its reform and opening up in 1978 China has leveraged its cultural and tourism sector to stimulate consumption, foster job creation, and significantly improve the country’s economic structure by integrating tourism into other industries to create new demand and business models. The plan set a goal to attract 190 million inbound tourists annually by 2030, with more than $150 billion inbound tourism spending a year.

Given the size of China’s market, its efforts will be crucial to the ongoing recovery of the global tourism industry. 
In 2025 an estimated 1.52 billion international tourists were recorded worldwide, nearly 60 million more than in 2024, marking 4 percent year-on-year growth. That’s almost a return to the 5 percent pre-pandemic growth trend. The latest World Tourism Barometer by U.N. Tourism attributed the positive results to several factors, namely strong demand, robust performance from large source markets, ongoing recovery of destinations in Asia and the Pacific, expanded air connectivity, and enhanced visa facilitation.

articles.title: SCO at 25: Institutionalizing Coexistence Without Convergence
articles.full_text:
In an international system increasingly characterized by strategic distrust, contested borders, fragmented and overlapping alignments, the capacity to communicate with one’s rivals remains critical for conflict management.
When the leaders of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) gather in Bishkek on September 1, 2026, they will be celebrating a quarter-century journey: from an original six members in 2001 to now the world’s largest regional organization comprising 10 members – China, Russia, India, Pakistan, Iran, Belarus, and four Central Asian republics – with Afghanistan and Mongolia as observers, plus 15 dialogue partners stretching from from the South Caucasus to the Middle East, South, and Southeast Asia.
But the 25th anniversary will also be an occasion for a reality check. At first glance, persistent intra-SCO tensions are clear: Russia has dragged Belarus into its war with Ukraine; Iran’s war with the United States has seen it attacking Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia; Afghanistan and Pakistan are engaged in a cross-border conflict; India and China have an unresolved border and occasional military tensions; India and Pakistan have a deeply adversarial relationship; and Cambodia just last year was embroiled in a border war with Thailand. All of these states are either members, observers, or dialogue partners in the SCO.
Given that SCO specifically does not address bilateral problems, it has made no contribution to mitigating conflicts that, nevertheless, continue to complicate SCO deliberations. The question, therefore, is inevitable: what has the SCO achieved in the last 25 years? The answer may not be spectacular yet it remains critical for understanding Eurasia’s future trajectories. The SCO has institutionalized a unique experiment in building coexistence without convergences.
The SCO’s expanded membership and agenda surely remain its most visible source of relevance. Its original purpose was comparatively narrow: confidence-building and border management among China, Russia, and the Central Asian states. But today it operates across a variety of areas: countering terrorism, separatism, and extremism; addressing narcotics and organized crime; cybersecurity; energy; transport and connectivity; trade and investment; finance; science and technology; artificial intelligence; culture; tourism; education; and youth empowerment.
The SCO’s Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS) began in Tashkent in 2004 and its Peace Mission military exercises from 2003. Today, its ecosystem includes a secretariat, working groups, and other specialized mechanisms covering businesses, banking, youth, and academia. 
But its expansion has not translated into trust building. The SCO’s Charter itself stresses principles of sovereignty, non-interference, and equality, while seeking common positions only on matters of mutual interest. It is therefore structurally ill-equipped to mediate bilateral disputes that continue to undermine convergences.
It is also important to underline that the SCO has evolved less as a NATO-like alliance or EU-like union and more as a security community. The ideal type of security community, in the vein of Karl Deutsch, grows around the “expectation” that members would settle disputes through “peaceful change.” Emanuel Adler and Michael Barnett placed trust, mutual identification, communication, and dependable expectations at the heart of “mature” security communities. For decades, ASEAN has been striving to achieve this dream. For the SCO as well, building that kind of trust has remained an arduous undertaking.
International relations experts usually assume multilateral forums will produce a virtuous progression: repeated interactions create familiarity; familiarity encourages confidence-building; confidence generates trust; trust facilitates cooperation; cooperation gradually creates convergences. The SCO’s track record offers a strikingly different trajectory: from distrust to institutionalizing predictable interactions to selective cooperation, all while distrust persists.
The SCO has not solved the trust deficit; it has papered over it with bureaucracy. Rivals continue to meet through councils of heads of state and foreign ministers, national coordinators, working groups, security agencies, military exercises, and sector specific forums. RATS remains its most enduring mechanism for counterterrorism cooperation. The Peace Mission exercises and anti-narcotics cooperation have become increasingly robust. The SCO reported that its August 2025 Spider Web operation resulted in the seizure of more than 9 tonnes of narcotics and more than 21 tonnes of precursors.
This institutionalization gives adversaries routines and avenues to keep interacting. They have not forgotten their conflicts but do not allow those conflicts to destroy this institutional rhythm. It speaks to the SCO’s inherent strength and solidarity, granting it resilience even as its members include states that are simultaneously competitors, adversaries, and security partners. The glue is not trust but a shared habit of institutionalized interactions where distrust is often factored in and endured.
The SCO has evolved less as a conventional organization and more into an ecosystem for building a security community. Its extraordinary diversity, especially of regime types and size, makes consensus its greatest constraint but also its core asset. Consensus prevents any single power from converting the SCO into a geopolitical instrument. It allows China, Russia, India, Pakistan, and Iran to remain inside the same framework despite profound differences.
But consensus also has its costs. The SCO can accommodate disagreement because it rarely requires members to give up their core interests. The result? It produces open-ended declarations with few binding collective actions. The SCO does not ask for common strategic identity or shared political values, nor interfere in members’ bilateral disputes. This is by design and undergirds SCO’s longevity.
The SCO’s network of specialized bodies, observer missions, business and banking institutions, security mechanisms and external relationships matter more than the formal organization itself. The SCO, for instance, has managed 76 election-observer missions since 2004 and maintains close relationships with the U.N. and multiple other regional organizations. The SCO may not have produced convergence but it has ingrained among its members a habit of meeting, consulting, and exchanging information despite distrust.
Tianjin to Bishkek: Summitry vs. Delivery
This approach should moderate our expectations from Bishkek. At the Tianjin SCO summit last year, leaders agreed to establish an Anti-Drug Center in Dushanbe and a Universal Center for Countering Security Challenges and Threats in Tashkent. They decided to replace separate categories of “observer” and “dialogue partner” with a single “SCO partner” status. The Bishkek summit is expected to deliver on each of these proposals.
The Tianjin summit kickstarted negotiations to ratify the required amendments the SCO’s legal frameworks but this may take some time. The idea of an Anti-Drug Center has moved into the preparatory implementation stage and, by May 2026, SCO anti-narcotics officials had approved a working draft to be submitted to the Bishkek summit. The Tianjin summit had also agreed in principle to the establishment of an SCO Development Bank, but it continues to face consensus-building challenges as it has since it was first suggested in 2010.
It is tempting to expect the Bishkek summit to turn these promises into reality. But should the SCO’s credibility be judged by this yardstick alone or how many new declarations emerge from Bishkek? Remember, the SCO’s real strength lies in its members having “moved” from old fashioned leaving-the-room when interests diverge to innovative ways of keeping the door open.
The Bishkek summit should not be judged by whether the SCO can resolve the dispute over Kashmir or the India-China border, whether it can settle Afghanistan-Pakistan tensions or address wider conflicts involving Russia and Iran. Nor should its success be measured simply by counting members, partners, summits, or declarations. Its greatest success is that, after 25 years, the SCO has created something distinctive: an institutional architecture in which strategic competitors can coexist without converging.
SCO members and partners may not have become friends. They have, however, built enough institutional resilience to keep their tensions from automatically destroying their shared forum. This may sound rather modest. The SCO’s achievement, thus, may not be what it has brought its members to agree upon. It instead lies in how the SCO has trained them to live together, even without trust.

articles.title: AI, Scams, the Law, and Governance: A Conversation With David Tan
articles.full_text:
How are Southeast Asia’s governments facing up to the challenges of AI?
Governments across Southeast Asia are struggling with the arrival of artificial intelligence, both its endless possibilities that can improve everyday life and the threats posed by organized crime and the scam industries that have taken hold in the region.
Singapore-based David Tan, co-director of the Centre for Technology, Robotics, Artificial Intelligence & the Law, says the predominant issues evolve around what he calls the three Ps: permanence, proliferation, and perniciousness. 
“We only need to regulate what’s truly important – what’s really pernicious, that proliferates, and has that permanent digital memory,” he said, adding: “Intimate sexual images, child abuse images, whether digital or not, that should be a priority.”
Tan, who also heads Intellectual Property at the EW Barker Centre for Law & Business at the National University of Singapore, spoke with The Diplomat’s Luke Hunt about how to combat the negative impact and AI’s reach into financial markets, public health, and pop culture.
Common law and legislation are key, as are online safety commissions. These commissions have been deployed by a core group of eight countries, Singapore and South Korea among them, where national authorities coordinate across borders through the Global Online Safety Regulators Network.
But Tan said the industrialized scam industry is here to stay, with crime syndicates expected to grow and continue taking advantage of AI and in particular, deep fakes.
“I think that one just has to be more vigilant as to the kind of fakes we get,” he said.

articles.title: The Tibet-Nepal Flood Is a Himalayan Climate Security Warning
articles.full_text:
The catastrophic flood this week proves that Tibet needs to be at the center of international climate security discussions.
A flooded village in Rasuwa District, Nepal, Aug. 26, 2026.
The catastrophic flash flood that struck the Tibet-Nepal border on August 26 should not be treated simply as another Himalayan natural disaster. It is better understood as a warning from a rapidly destabilizing cryosphere, one that transcends political borders. The disaster exposed the growing collision between climate change, geological fragility, infrastructure expansion, and weak transboundary environmental governance. 
What happened along the Nepal-Tibet frontier reinforces an argument that climate researchers have increasingly made: the Himalayan-Tibetan ecosystem must be approached not merely as an environmental space but as a critical arena of transboundary climate and cryosphere security.
Initial reports suggested that an earthquake had triggered the disaster. Subsequent analysis by the U.S. Geological Survey indicated something different: the seismic signal was generated by the collapse itself, rather than a preceding tectonic earthquake. A large section of a high-altitude glacier – located at roughly 5,200 meters in elevation – broke away and plunged approximately 1,200 meters toward the valley floor. The resulting ice-rock avalanche entrained enormous quantities of debris and appears to have temporarily obstructed the Lhende Khola River before releasing a devastating surge downstream. 
The tragedy was not simply a conventional flood produced by excessive rainfall. Nor does the evidence currently justify describing it as an earthquake-triggered disaster. It was a cascading high-mountain event in which ice, rock, gravity, water, and steep topography combined. The narrow Himalayan valleys then acted as conduits for an exceptionally fast-moving mixture of water, sediment, and boulders. 
The disaster therefore raises two questions that should extend well beyond its immediate aftermath. How safe is the accelerating infrastructure expansion across Tibet when the geological and cryospheric foundations of the plateau are becoming increasingly unstable? And when environmental disturbances originating in Tibet can rapidly become disasters in Nepal and other downstream states, should Tibet’s climate crisis continue to be treated primarily as China’s domestic environmental concern?
The science points toward a much larger problem. The Hindu Kush Himalayan cryosphere is changing at an extraordinary pace. Glaciers are retreating, snow patterns are changing, and permafrost is degrading. The mountain slopes are becoming increasingly vulnerable to complex interactions among temperature, precipitation, meltwater, seismic activity, and gravity. These changes can generate avalanches, debris flows, landslides, glacial lake outburst floods, and other cascading and interrelated hazards.
The Tibet-Nepal tragedy therefore needs to be understood not as an isolated incident but as part of an emerging pattern of compound Himalayan hazards. The same broad border region has witnessed repeated episodes in which events originating at high altitude have rapidly translated into downstream emergencies. In July 2025, for example, a devastating flood in Nepal’s Bhotekoshi River was traced by satellite analysis to the drainage of a supraglacial lake in Tibet. That disaster destroyed the Friendship Bridge connecting Nepal and China and caused casualties and substantial infrastructure damage.
There is an important geopolitical lesson here: the physical geography of a degrading cryosphere transcends political borders.
This is precisely why Tibet matters. The Tibetan Plateau is the hydrological heart of Asia and the source region for major river systems on which enormous downstream populations depend. What happens to its glaciers, permafrost, lakes, slopes and rivers inevitably carries consequences beyond China’s administrative boundaries. A glacial collapse, landslide or sudden water release in an upstream area can become a disaster in another country within hours. 
Our Stockholm Paper “Whither Tibet in the Climate Crisis Agenda?” sought to draw attention to precisely this structural vulnerability. The study argued that Tibet is undergoing one of the world’s most consequential yet insufficiently scrutinized ecological transformations. We called for greater international attention to the interaction among climate change, infrastructure, resource extraction, water governance, and regional security. 
Our paper deliberately rejected a narrow understanding of Tibet’s climate crisis as merely an issue of pollution or glacier retreat. Instead, infrastructure expansion, extractive activities, and governance choices can interact with accelerating cryospheric transformation to create risks extending far beyond Tibet itself. The latest tragedy makes that warning considerably harder to ignore.
Infrastructure is particularly important in this discussion, although scientific caution is essential. No conclusive evidence currently shows that a particular Chinese infrastructure project directly caused the August 26 glacier collapse. Making such a claim would go beyond the available data. Researchers are still examining the precise combination of temperature changes, snowmelt, glacier dynamics, permafrost degradation, slope instability, and geological factors involved. But even while we await concrete data on this one disaster, the broader infrastructure problem is plain to see.
The Tibetan Plateau and surrounding Himalayas constitute an exceptionally difficult environment for large-scale construction. Steep topography, active tectonics, retreating glaciers, thawing permafrost and unstable slopes increasingly overlap with roads, railways, hydropower facilities, border infrastructure, settlements, mining activities, and other strategic projects. Infrastructure is consequently being built on landscapes whose physical behavior is becoming more difficult to predict. 
This produces a dangerous paradox. Infrastructure itself is increasingly vulnerable to climate and geological hazards, even while badly located or inadequately assessed construction can magnify exposure to those hazards. Road cutting and excavation can destabilize slopes. Tunnelling, blasting and mining can disturb already fragile geological environments. Hydropower installations and dams concentrate workers, equipment, and economic assets in narrow river corridors precisely where debris flows and flash floods can travel with extraordinary force. 
The concern therefore should not be framed simplistically as development versus environmental protection. The more urgent question is whether development models designed for comparatively stable physical environments remain appropriate for a high-altitude landscape undergoing rapid climatic transformation.
Scientists are not demanding an indiscriminate halt to every infrastructure project in Tibet, but more care is needed. Major construction in exceptionally fragile cryospheric zones should be subjected to far more rigorous precautionary scrutiny, including independent hazard mapping, cumulative environmental-impact assessments, permafrost and glacier monitoring, downstream risk analysis, and transparent disaster modelling. Where the risks cannot reasonably be mitigated, restrictions or outright bans on new constructions should become legitimate policy options.
China’s expanding infrastructure footprint across Tibet makes this particularly consequential. The issue is not simply what this infrastructure – and the intersecting disaster risks – may do to Tibet. Increasingly, it is also what a changing Tibet means for countries and peoples living downstream.
Nepal Cannot Remain Downstream Diplomatically
For Nepal, this creates an uncomfortable strategic reality. Kathmandu cannot afford to view infrastructure and environmental decision-making north of its border exclusively through the prism of China-Nepal economic cooperation. Nepal is geographically downstream from climatic and hydrological processes over which it exercises little control. Its vulnerability therefore produces a legitimate diplomatic interest in developments occurring on the Tibetan side of the frontier. 
Timely information sharing on the upstream environment should not be regarded as diplomatic generosity from China. For Nepal, it can literally save lives. Kathmandu consequently has strong grounds to demand more institutionalized transboundary consultation, real-time hydrological information, glacier and glacial lake monitoring, advance notification of significant upstream projects, joint disaster risk assessments, and emergency communication mechanisms with Beijing. 
Such demands should not automatically be interpreted as anti-China. This is elementary risk management for a downstream Himalayan state. 
Nepal should likewise be cautious about allowing infrastructure diplomacy to overshadow environmental security. Chinese roads, connectivity projects, border facilities, energy investments, and other infrastructure can provide economic opportunities. But their value cannot be measured solely through investment volumes, construction kilometers, or trade projections; the risks must also be carefully weighed.
This principle extends beyond Nepal. Bhutan, India and other downstream Himalayan states have legitimate interests in greater transparency concerning upstream environmental changes. The concept of territorial control cannot mean that a state possesses exclusive political control over territory while neighboring countries are expected to absorb the environmental consequences without adequate consultation. That is precisely where transboundary cryosphere security becomes a useful diplomatic concept. 
The issue consequently belongs on a much larger international agenda. The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and wider international climate architecture should give far greater attention to the Himalayas and cryosphere security. Existing discussions acknowledge glacier retreat, snow cover changes, permafrost degradation, and adaptation challenges. Yet the Tibet-Nepal tragedy demonstrates why the agenda must move from general recognition toward sustained monitoring, risk assessment, and transboundary adaptation mechanisms. Tibet should not remain an environmental blind spot within global climate diplomacy simply because discussion of the plateau is politically sensitive. 
Climate systems do not observe sovereignty in the manner diplomatic institutions do. A flood originating in Tibet can become an emergency in Nepal and potentially affect communities much farther downstream. This is where a new diplomatic conversation is required. The objective should not be to internationalize Tibet politically under the guise of climate change. It should instead be to internationalize responsibility for understanding and managing transboundary climate risks in the Himalayan region. 
China, Nepal, India, Bhutan and other Himalayan stakeholders need stronger arrangements for cryosphere data sharing, joint scientific observation, satellite based early warning, infrastructure risk assessments, and disaster preparedness. Institutions such as Nepal’s International Center for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) can provide scientific platforms where such cooperation is framed around environmental security and human safety rather than geopolitical confrontation. 
But international institutions also have responsibilities. The UNFCCC process should encourage systematic discussion of the Tibetan Plateau and Himalayan cryosphere within adaptation, loss-and-damage, and mountain ecosystem frameworks. Greater international scientific access, transparent environmental data, and systematic assessment of major infrastructure projects in environmentally sensitive transboundary regions should become part of that conversation. 
The August 26 tragedy should mark a turning point. The international community needs to stop treating Tibet’s environmental transformation as a distant ecological issue. The plateau is becoming one of Asia’s central climate security theaters, where warming, glaciers, permafrost, seismicity, infrastructure and geopolitics increasingly intersect. The catastrophic flood this week proves that beyond question. Tibet must therefore move from the margins toward the center of international climate security discussions.
articles.summary: The catastrophic flood this week proves that Tibet needs to be at the center of international climate security discussions.

articles.title: Nepal’s ‘Himalayan Tsunami’ Is a Warning for the Whole Region
articles.full_text:
Melting ice, unstable terrain, landslides, river blockages, sudden lake releases, and extreme weather can all combine in unpredictable ways.
A screenshot of CCTV footage shows the moment that a massive mudslide engulfed the town of Gyirong in Tibet, China, Aug. 26, 2026.
For Nepali people, August 26 started like any other day, just another routine morning for the communities in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, and Chitwan. But there is a saying in Nepal: “Disaster won’t come by making noise.” On Wednesday, people experienced that reality ruthlessly.
By midday, that ordinary morning had turned into a nightmare. A sudden flood that crashed down from the northern side of the border devastated multiple districts of Nepal. The customs office of the Nepal-China border, Syaphrubeshi, Betrawati, Timure, and Trisuli area in Rasuwa district all suffered extensive damage. Entire villages were swept away. The floodwaters then rushed toward the Trishuli River, threatening more settlements in the areas of Nuwakot and Dhading.
Over 30 bridges collapsed, 42 kilometers of roads were damaged or simply washed away, and communications were disrupted. Thousands of homes were swept away. More than 359 bodies have been recovered so far, and there are still thousands of locals missing. In addition, more than 644 tourists from 33 countries were reported missing. Security personnel themselves were reported missing. 
In China also, at least three people were killed and more than 500 people were reported missing. In both countries, rescue and recovery operations are ongoing.
What exactly caused the disaster is still unclear, but experts believe a massive avalanche or landslide may have blocked the river, creating a temporary dam that eventually burst. It could have been a glacial lake outburst flood – if confirmed, that would be a warning for the entire Hindu Kush Himalayan region about the growing threat of climate crises. 
By 3:30 p.m. on Wednesday, the Bhotekoshi River had receded and returned to its original size. But that only made clear the devastation it had wreaked throughout the morning. There was not a trace left of the villages, market towns, bridges, or hydroelectric projects that had once stood along the riverbanks. It is estimated that in one morning the Bhotekoshi washed away over 200 billion rupees worth of investment: roads and bridges were devastated, and neither the hydropower projects nor the transmission lines survived. This is worrisome for a small economy like Nepal. 
The Nepal government has declared Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts as disaster crisis zones for the next three months. 
While the initial flood has passed, there are still worrying signs coming from China. China’s Ministry of Water Resources warned that a 2 million cubic meter lake near the Chhochen Khola-Purepu Tsangpo confluence is already overflowing, with another 3 million cubic meters expected to flow in, posing a high risk of breach. That could cause a second flood at any time.
Wednesday’s disaster marked the second time in just over a year that Nepal’s Rasuwa district has been devastated by a catastrophic flood, and once again, the disaster didn’t start within its borders. In July 2025, a similar flood in the same region wiped out the Rasuwagadhi border corridor. Satellite images later showed that a glacial lake in Tibet had drained suddenly. At least 11 people were killed in the 2025 flood, which also destroyed bridges, damaged energy infrastructure, and disrupted cross-border trade with China. 
Now, just 13 months later, history has repeated itself. That’s not a coincidence. 
Professor Ranjan Kumar Dahal of Tribhuvan University said that this is the largest ice tsunami in the last 50 years – not just in Nepal, but across the entire Himalayan region. Whether this turns out to be a glacial lake outburst flood, a landslide-triggered flood, or a mix of both, one thing is clear: the danger is growing, and the damage won’t be limited to any one country.
The devastating flood on Nepal’s Bhotekoshi River was the result of a “massive geological event” in the Himalayas. As per Goran Ekstrom, a geophysicist at Columbia University’s Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, the event was triggered by a catastrophic chain of occurrences in the Himalayan region.
Nepal’s area of the Himalayas holds an estimated 2,069 to 2,174 glacial lakes. According to the International Center for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), 47 of these are classified as potentially dangerous glacial lakes, capable of triggering catastrophic outburst floods. Among these 47 glacial lakes, 21 lie within Nepal, while 25 are transboundary lakes in Tibet, sitting right at the headwaters of rivers that flow south into Nepal. If any of the lakes, whether in Tibet or Nepal, cause an outburst flood, this will harm the people and infrastructure of Nepal living downstream.
Across the Hindu Kush Himalaya, rising temperatures are reshaping the frozen landscape. Glaciers are shrinking, lakes are swelling, and mountain slopes are growing more unstable. The ICIMOD has repeatedly warned that glacier-related disasters are becoming more frequent and more complex.
Experts can’t yet say with perfect confidence that climate change directly caused this week’s flood. But it is changing the rules of the game. The new reality isn’t just about more floods, but about cascading threats. Melting ice, unstable terrain, landslides, river blockages, sudden lake releases, and extreme weather can all combine in unpredictable ways. Conventional weather monitoring downstream just isn’t enough anymore.
This can’t be seen as a matter of the environment but also a matter of national security. The affected corridor is at once a lifeline for communities, a trade artery, an energy source, and a strategic border zone.
There is growing hope for positive change in Nepal’s disaster response. Both Prime Minister Balendra Shah and Physical Infrastructure Minister Sunil Lamsal have backgrounds in structural engineering, and Home Minister Sudan Gurung has experience in relief work. The country can’t stop every Himalayan disaster, but the government can make sure fewer people are caught standing by the river when the mountain unleashes its fury. The real challenge is anticipating these events before they strike.
This is not a problem Nepal can solve on its own. The Bhotekoshi River begins in Tibet and flows into Nepal. A hazard born on the Chinese side can become a national emergency in Nepal within hours. Nepal’s ability to prepare depends almost entirely on getting timely information from across the border.
Likewise, there are millions of people living downstream on the same rivers in both Nepal and India. If a glacial lake bursts in Tibet or Nepal, it will also impact and cause severe harm in India too. So this has also become an urgent cross-border problem. The countries from the Hindu Kush Himalayan region must work together to combat this kind of disaster in a timely manner before it becomes too late. Climate diplomacy in the Himalayas can’t just be about emissions and funding anymore. It has to include real-time data sharing, satellite surveillance of risky glacial and landslide-dammed lakes, joint risk assessments, and rapid cross-border early warning systems. 
For Nepal, this is the worst natural disaster since the 2015 earthquake. Despite contributing less than 0.1 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, Nepal is facing disproportionate environmental and economic consequences. Big neighbors like India and China and partner countries must help Nepal in every possible way. The 2025 flood was a wake-up call. The 2026 flood is a blunt reminder that it wasn’t a one-off.
The message is becoming painfully clear: resilience cannot simply mean rebuilding what the river takes away. It means knowing what is happening upstream before the water arrives. Climate change is real and not a hoax, and Nepal cannot face these growing risks alone. Stronger regional cooperation, shared technology, and global support are important and necessary parts of the response to this tragedy.
