articles.title: Rahul Gandhi Ushers a New Style of Youth-Centric Politics in India
articles.full_text:
From being mocked for being inexperienced and incompetent, he is now emerging a sought-after leader of India’s youth.
A screengrab of an Indian National Congress video of Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi addressing youth at the Chhatron ki Goonj event in Pune, India, Aug. 22, 2026.
When Congress leader and Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi addressed women students at the Chhatron ki Goonj (Voice of Students) event in Pune last week, he urged them to “Smash the Patriarchy,” a message that resonated not just with his audience at the Pune event but with youth across the country.
“India’s biggest strength, its asset,” Gandhi said, “is its 70 crore (700 million) women.”
“Be loud, be proud. Fight for your space,” he told his young audience.
Unsurprisingly, his speech raised the hackles of India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). BJP leader and Union Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Kiren Rijiju questioned why Gandhi was “always target[ing] only Hindu? What about minority women…”
Gandhi had not mentioned Hindus in his speech. However, the BJP, a Hindu nationalist party, chose to misquote the Congress leader in a bid to shift the discourse to a Hindu-Muslim communal one, a standard ploy of the BJP and other Hindutva organizations.
Since the protests at New Delhi’s Jantar Mantar in June-July this year, India’s Gen Z has shown utter disdain for the BJP and its leaders and the kind of politics they engage in. Indeed, several protestors used expletives to mock BJP leaders.
In a desperate attempt to win back their support, Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressed Gen Z youth for the first time on the night of July 24 through an awkward hand-held Instagram reel, where he said he was “pained” and it was a “cultural shock” seeing “our young daughters” mouthing expletives against him and other BJP leaders. Modi’s speech was condescending. He spoke down to the protesters, viewing them through a patriarchal lens and addressing them as his daughters and sisters. He described them as “misguided” and said he had “forgiven” them.
Modi’s speech infuriated Gen Z in general and women in particular, who have continued to target the BJP and its patriarchal mindset.
The BJP and its ideological mentor, the Rashtriya Swayamsewak Sangh (RSS), are intensely patriarchal organizations led by geriatric men steeped in conservatism and misogyny. They are seriously out of touch with India’s educated youth.
Gandhi’s speech at Pune on August 22 was undoubtedly aimed at presenting himself as a foil to Modi’s patriarchal image. He drew the attention of youth to the BJP’s patriarchal and gender discriminatory mindset.  While Modi called out women for using expletives at the Jantar Mantar protests, he was not similarly “pained” by the abusive language of male protesters, Gandhi pointed out.
Gandhi appears to be seeking to change the political discourse in India, shifting it away from the BJP’s communal discourse to one that strikes a chord with youth in general and women in particular. He is leveraging youth power in a big way by speaking about youth aspirations and problems.
Following the widespread outrage among students over the leakage of question papers of the NEET entrance exam, Gandhi began the Chhatron ki Goonj campaign in various cities, where he spoke about the exam paper leak extortion racket, unemployment, educational degrees without jobs, and the private coaching mafia. The events drew large crowds.
Then in June-July, the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) started protests at Jantar Mantar, which drew thousands of students to the protest site. The Modi government’s use of force against the protesters on July 20 galvanized the students. The Jantar Mantar protests were successful in forcing Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign, a key demand of the protests. This was the first time in 12 years since Modi and the BJP came to power that mass protests were able to force the resignation of a sitting minister.
Following the police brutality on July 20, which saw police use pellet guns on protesters, Gandhi led a dharna (a sit-in protest) in front of the prime minister’s residence. It led to a confrontation that left Gandhi with a bloody nose; the visuals went viral on social media. For both the CJP students and the Leftist student unions that participated in the Jantar Mantar protests, this was a rare occasion of a leading politician not only raising their issues in parliament but also taking the fight to the streets. Not surprisingly, prominent youth leaders like Neha Bora were happy to address the media, alongside Gandhi.
Gandhi aligned himself with Gen Z in Parliament; the Congress-led opposition parties did not allow Parliament to function during the recent monsoon session and demanded the resignation of Home Minister Amit Shah for sanctioning police brutality on the students. Gandhi actively took up the case of a pellet gun victim at Jantar Mantar, 19-year-old Sahil Lochab, a student protester, who was so severely injured by the pellets fired by police that he lost his vision in one eye. With the Delhi Police refusing to lodge a complaint in this case for over a month, Gandhi, last week, spent over seven hours at the local police station and refused to leave until the complaint was lodged.
With India’s mainstream media functioning more or less as mouthpieces of the Modi government, the student protesters have relied on social media and YouTube channels of independent journalists to convey the picture on the ground. They boycotted mainstream TV news channels that were trying to defame their protests.  Through live videos, catchy slogans, memes, and Instagram reels using humor and satire, Gen Z garnered public attention and support. They fearlessly lampooned Modi’s strong man image, cultivated since 2014, with a meme of a baby monkey, which is still viral on social media.
In his outreach, Gandhi appears authentic, young, and tech-friendly. He is leveraging social media by posting short videos of his daily life and sharing his thoughts through Instagram reels and YouTube videos that have made him more relatable to a young audience. Unlike Modi, who has never held a press conference in the 12 years he has been India’s prime minister, and addresses audiences only with the help of a teleprompter, Gandhi seems an approachable leader. Not only has he held press conferences and spoken to the media candidly, but he has also opened up to youth via Ask Me Anything sessions. He has shown willingness to engage with youth as equals and does not preach to them.
Unlike Modi’s Insta reel debut on the night of July 24, which backfired spectacularly with Gen Z, Gandhi’s relatable outreach is striking a chord with youngsters
Fifty-five-year-old Gandhi does not pretend to be young; he asks youngsters to teach him Gen Z lingo. He asks them about their aspirations and how he can better understand their problems. He is not insecure about his masculinity and wears pink and yellow colored shirts, usually seen as feminine colors.
In its 12th year in power and despite enjoying a majority in parliament, the BJP is rattled. It is out of sync with youth, who comprise 30 percent of India’s electorate.
The BJP’s IT Cell, which was infamous for trolling and doxxing dissenters and critics on social media, is in trouble as it failed to anticipate and grasp the Gen Z mood during the student protests. Amit Malviya, who headed the BJP’s IT cell, was recently shunted out.
Despite these setbacks, Modi’s inability to course-correct is evident. In his Independence Day speech on August 15, he ranted against “Dimagi Naxal” (intellectual or thinking leftist rebels), which served as a dog whistle to right-wing goons and BJP-affiliated students to attack leftist academics at Jadavpur University in West Bengal.
Modi also issued diktats to Cabinet ministers to make Instagram reels and posts, without addressing the content of what youth are angry about. The CJP shot back, urging the government to pay attention to their “School Theek Karo”(Repair the Schools) campaign across the country and take remedial action. “They’ll spend money on anything and everything, just not on schools,” the CJP’s Abhijeet Dipke posted on X.
Interestingly, Gandhi’s image has evolved from being mocked pejoratively as “Pappu” (inexperienced or incompetent) to becoming the most sought-after leader of India’s youth. He has emerged as the perfect foil to Modi’s jaded and arrogant image. In fact, leaders of other opposition parties, including Akhilesh Yadav of the Samajwadi Party, have started adapting to the new style of politics that Gandhi has ushered in.
When Congress leader and Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi addressed women students at the Chhatron ki Goonj (Voice of Students) event in Pune last week, he urged them to “Smash the Patriarchy,” a message that resonated not just with his audience at the Pune event but with youth across the country.
“India’s biggest strength, its asset,” Gandhi said, “is its 70 crore (700 million) women.”
“Be loud, be proud. Fight for your space,” he told his young audience.
Unsurprisingly, his speech raised the hackles of India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). BJP leader and Union Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Kiren Rijiju questioned why Gandhi was “always target[ing] only Hindu? What about minority women…”
articles.summary: From being mocked for being inexperienced and incompetent, he is now emerging a sought-after leader of India’s youth.

Whether dressed in traditional thanakas, dresses, or burqas, their message was the same.
A banner tells the story of Rohingya homes and villages burning, families fleeing, and lives being lost. It’s a reminder of what happened and why the Rohingya continue to seek justice, safety, dignity, and the right to return home.
With tear-filled eyes, Rohingya teachers and activists spoke of a homeland scarred by genocide, families separated, loved ones lost and a people waiting for justice.
Rohingya leaders speak with grief, courage, and determination on Aug. 25, 2026, keeping alive the memory of those killed and the call for justice and safe return.
A Rohingya father carries his young son on his shoulders as he heads towards Rohingya Genocide Remembrance Day. The child is one of many growing up in the refugee camp with no memories of his homeland.
Unable to find a place in the crowded gathering, Rohingya refugees watch from afar, remembering their lost loved ones and homeland.
A Rohingya youth shares a water bottle with his fellow Rohingya girls, a simple act of care and solidarity in the middle of the crowd.
Rohingya refugees walk together to commemorate the ninth anniversary of the Rohingya genocide, Aug. 25, 2026.
In collective prayers, Rohingya refugees break down in tears, remember their lost loved ones, pray for justice, and hope for the day they return home safely.
Every year on August 25, the Rohingya community around the world gather to commemorate Rohingya Genocide Remembrance Day. It is a day of mourning, expression, reflection, and hope. On this day, Rohingya people living abroad and in refugee camps hold banners, join together for mass prayers, recite poems, share their history, organize refugee exhibitions, and participate in social activities. 
All of these activities aim to remember their homeland and memories, and to honor their loved ones who were killed by the Myanmar authorities on August 25, 2017.
For the Rohingya, August 25 is not just a black day. It is a day that has buried countless innocent Rohingya, that has mixed the tears of the Rohingya with blood, and that has forced more than a million Rohingya to flee to Bangladesh. On this day, the Myanmar military put into motion its plan to wipe out the Rohingya community from Myanmar’s Rakhine State under the pretext of responding to an attack on a police station.
According to international human rights groups and Rohingya civil society organizations, more than 300 Rohingya villages were partially or completely destroyed following the Myanmar military’s attacks beginning on August 25, 2017. Rohingya women and girls were raped in front of their parents, husbands, and brothers. Children were thrown into fires, and people were burned to death inside their homes. Many were arrested and sent to jail; many family members still don’t know the whereabouts of their jailed family members. Property was looted, and mosques were destroyed. Many died after their trawlers were capsized or broken in the Naf River while fleeing to Bangladesh. 
Doctors Without Borders concluded that “[a]t least 9,000 members of the ethnic Rohingya minority died – most of them from violence – in Rakhine State, Myanmar” in the month after the violence began on August 25, 2017. 
“I witnessed the brutal massacre of my Rohingya community by the Myanmar military in 2017. The bullets that flew over my head were like raindrops,” Rohingya teacher Wai Yan recounted during a Rohingya Genocide Remembrance Day event. “All I saw were dead bodies with no one to bury them.”
This year, August 25 marked the ninth anniversary of the violence, but the pain has not yet subsided. The Rohingya who fled are still trapped in overcrowded camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, waiting for justice from the world, while the remaining Rohingya in Myanmar continue to suffer from an ongoing genocide by the Arakan Army. 
The suffering never ended for the Rohingya. The Arakan Army is fighting Myanmar’s military for control of Rakhine State, and both groups have been attacking Rohingya villages – killing, looting, and burning. Many Rohingya have been killed, women have been raped, homes looted and burned to the ground, often with the occupants inside. 
After the military genocide against the Rohingya earlier, they are now facing similar treatment from the Arakan Army. According to a report by Human Rights Watch, the Arakan Army has targeted Rohingya civilians through killings, unlawful detention, forced recruitment of Rohingya youths, and other abuses that may amount to war crimes. Many Rohingya believe that the brutality carried out by the Arakan Army is aimed at driving the Rohingya out of the country, just like the Myanmar military’s campaign in 2017. 
Nine years have passed since the Rohingya were driven from their homeland, but the possibility for return remains fragile; not a single Rohingya has returned through the repatriation process since 2017. Bangladesh – a small and densely populated country – continues to shoulder the responsibility of hosting refugees.
Bangladesh had previously tried to repatriate Rohingya, but their efforts failed. The refugees will not return as long as their safety, rights, and dignity are uncertain. Humanitarian assistance has helped the Rohingya endure their displacement, but the root causes of the crisis can only be addressed through political action. Myanmar must recognize the Rohingya as native people of Myanmar and create the conditions for their safe, voluntary, and dignified return with citizenship and rights.
August 25 is not only about remembering what happened to the Rohingya in 2017. It is also about recognizing the challenges that continue today. Rohingya families remain trapped in the refugee camps, uncertain about their future. Children are growing up in the camps far from their homeland, learning about their homeland through the memories of their parents and grandparents.
articles.summary: Nine years on, Rohingya refugees still wait for justice and home. But they haven't given up hope.

articles.title: Flash Flood Devastates China-Nepal Border Region
articles.full_text:
The flood, centered on Nepal’s Rasuwa District and China’s Gyirong County, killed at least 160 people, with 900 still missing.
A flash flood tears through Nepal’s Rasuwa District, Aug. 26, 2026.
A devastating flash flood along the China-Nepal border has killed at least 160 people, with nearly a thousand more missing. The disaster centered on Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, including the trading hub of Syabrubesi on the border. On the Chinese side, Gyirong County in Tibet was hit.
According to Nepali officials, the flood began at 8:40 a.m. on August 26, just three minutes after a magnitude 4.4 earthquake hit in Tibet, on China’s side of the border. That apparently caused a landslide involving both rock and ice from a Himalayan glacier. When the material flowed into the Lhende River in Tibet, known in Nepal as the Bhotekoshi, it caused the river to catastrophically overflow its banks.
The Kathmandu Post summarized a Nepali-language explanation offered by Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA): 
The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said a preliminary study, based on an analysis of Planet Labs satellite imagery, indicates that a debris-laden flood entered the Lhende river after a glacial-rock slide occurred along the Nepal-China border, about 20 kilometres northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border point. The flood then flowed through Timure and entered the Trishuli river.
What exactly transformed a relatively minor earthquake into a crushing flood remains unclear. The Kathmandu Post reported that both Nepal and China were struggling to get accurate information in the immediate aftermath of the disaster. Citing Nepal’s consul general in Lhasa, the capital of Tibet, the Post said that “neither Nepali nor Chinese authorities had been able to establish contact with security personnel deployed along parts of the Nepal-China border. As a result, there was no authoritative information on what had triggered the massive outburst.”
Speculation centers on a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF), and for good reason: this particular kind of natural disaster has become more and more common in the Himalayan region in recent years. As glacial melt accelerates on our warming planet, the meltwater can become trapped behind debris, creating a new glacial lake. But if that natural dam breaks – perhaps under strain from a landslide, or shaken loose by an earthquake, or both – it releases a massive flood, along with all the debris that had been trapped.
A GLOF in India’s Sikkim in 2023 killed more than 100 people. The 2021 Uttarakhand flood, also in the Indian Himalayas, killed more than 200. Floods and landslides have become an annual occurrence in India’s Northeast, which borders both Nepal and China.
According to the latest statement from Nepal’s Office of the Prime Minister, 95 bodies have been recovered, many of which have yet to be identified. Hundreds of people are still missing, including 85 security personnel, 60 people “associated with various hydropower projects,” and 484 tourists (391 foreigners and 93 Nepalis). The tourists include 100 visitors from India, many of whom are in Nepal on a religious pilgrimage, 47 from the United States, and 33 from the United Kingdom.
Update: Nepal’s government has now confirmed 158 deaths, with over 400 people still missing.
Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority reported that nearly 200 people had been rescued from the affected area, with search and rescue operations ongoing. Videos posted online by the Nepal Police show a massive wall of water destroying a bridge and a town partially buried under mud.
As of this writing, China’s state-run broadcaster, CCTV, had confirmed only three deaths, but 265 people remain missing. Between China and Nepal, then, nearly 900 people are still unaccounted for, suggesting the death toll could rise sharply as recovery operations continue. 
General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party Xi Jinping, who is also China’s president, instructed local authorities “to make every effort to search for and rescue missing persons, relocate and resettle threatened people, and promptly treat the injured to minimize casualties,” according to CCTV. He also called for strengthening “monitoring and early warning systems.” While Xi didn’t mention it specifically, Nepali researchers have said a lack of timely information sharing about conditions on either side of the border may have contributed to the devastating impact.
In a post on Facebook, Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah said that the Nepali Army, Armed Police Force, and Nepal Police had been dispatched to the scene of the disaster “for rescue and relief operations.” 
In a follow-up post, Shah extended his “heartfelt” and “deepest condolences to those brothers and sisters who have mourned the loss of their people, their family, and everything.” He also had a message for the flood victims:
The pain you have suffered and the loss you have suffered is not small. But I want to assure you – you are not alone in these difficult times. The kingdom is with you all with its resources. Please be patient. The government will take full responsibility for your rescue, treatment, food, and shelter.
The flood will pose a test for Shah and his relatively new government. Shah took office as prime minister on March 27, 2026; he hadn’t quite reached the five-month mark before the disaster hit. A relative political neophyte, Shah was elected on a wave of anti-establishment sentiment after Gen Z protesters forced the previous government from office. But his lack of experience was already causing some headaches even before the flood.

articles.title: AI Is Lowering the Barriers to China’s Information Warfare Against Japan
articles.full_text:
China-linked influence operators are increasingly using AI to craft more effective disinformation campaigns.
Japan’s Ministry of Defense recently released its 2026 Defense of Japan white paper, once again drawing attention to China’s rapid advances in artificial intelligence and their implications for the regional security environment. Yet the most immediate danger to Japan may not come from AI’s application to conventional military systems. Generative AI is also lowering the barriers for Chinese information operations targeting Japanese society.
In late 2025, Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae made comments in the Diet linking a Taiwan contingency to Japan’s own security. Since then, disinformation targeting Japanese political figures and domestic issues has grown – not only in volume but also in sophistication. Research by organizations including the Sasakawa Peace Foundation and OpenAI suggests that China-linked influence operators are increasingly using AI to adapt their activities to Japan’s online environment and improve the efficiency of their operations.
AI is beginning to erode what was once one of the most obvious weaknesses of Chinese information operations against Japan: the linguistic and cultural barrier. Content that once featured grammatical mistakes, awkward translations and unnatural expressions is becoming harder for ordinary users to identify at a glance. 
If these capabilities are deployed to interfere with elections, discredit politicians or amplify social divisions, their effects could extend far beyond any single piece of false information.
A special report by Nikkei in February found that more than 400 China-linked social media accounts spread negative content about Takaichi during Japan’s House of Representatives election. Separately, the Yomiuri Shimbun, citing research by Japan Nexus Intelligence, reported that under a different set of criteria, thousands of coordinated accounts on X were involved in sharing and amplifying related content.
The narratives did not focus solely on attacking Takaichi personally. They also linked Japan’s efforts to strengthen its defense capabilities with concerns over social welfare, seeking to promote the argument that military expansion was coming at the expense of ordinary people.
In the past, such accounts often left obvious clues. Some had been created only recently. Their Japanese reflected Chinese word order and linguistic habits, while others mixed simplified Chinese characters with Japanese usage. AI-generated images also frequently contained visual errors that made them relatively easy to identify.
Those weaknesses, however, are becoming less pronounced.
The Sankei Shimbun has continued to track PAPERWALL, a China-linked information network that includes 15 websites masquerading as Japanese news outlets. The continued operation of these sites, and the broader ecosystem surrounding them, points toward an increasingly localized approach to influence operations. Improvements in language, imagery, and the appearance of fake news sites are making it more difficult for ordinary readers to distinguish legitimate sources from fabricated ones.
A report released by OpenAI in February offered another important clue. The company found that China-linked actors had used ChatGPT to assist in planning an online influence campaign targeting Takaichi. Influence actors appear willing to incorporate different AI systems into their existing workflows whenever those tools make their operations more effective.
What matters is not the nationality of the model. What matters is that generative AI is reducing the cost of cross-language information operations. In the past, producing large volumes of content tailored to a Japanese audience required translators, graphic designers, social media operators and people familiar with Japanese political and cultural contexts.
Large language models can now help operators correct grammar, adjust tone, generate images, and produce multiple versions of the same narrative for different audiences within minutes. In other words, AI is making China’s information warfare more scalable, faster and more localized.
How, then, should Japan respond? Taiwan offers one useful point of reference.
Taiwan has faced Chinese information operations for years and shares a Chinese-language environment with the mainland. Beijing therefore does not face the same linguistic barrier when targeting Taiwanese society that it encounters in Japan. Precisely for that reason, Taiwan was forced to develop social mechanisms for dealing with large-scale disinformation campaigns and networks of suspicious accounts.
Taiwan’s experience does not rely solely on government agencies or third-party fact-checkers. Individual users also identify, report, and block suspicious accounts, while civil society organizations and researchers continuously monitor information networks and patterns of coordinated behavior.
Language and culture themselves can also serve as tools for identifying manipulation. Although Taiwan and China both use Chinese, there are clear differences in vocabulary, grammar, social experience, and political context. Chinese influence operators can use AI to reduce these differences, but they cannot easily reproduce the cultural background and lived experience accumulated within another society.
Japan retains the same kind of advantage. Japanese language and social culture are highly contextual. Even if Chinese operators use AI to improve translation and content generation, that does not mean they can fully understand the linguistic and political differences between generations, regions, and social groups in Japan.
Japan should therefore move beyond a defensive model that waits for false information to appear and then fact-checks it. The more important task is to strengthen society’s ability to recognize coordinated influence operations before they gain traction.
This is also why information-security cooperation between Japan and Taiwan should become more institutionalized. The two sides could deepen exchanges on identifying coordinated accounts, detecting deepfakes, analyzing foreign influence networks and monitoring information environments during major disasters, elections, or political crises.
AI is making Chinese information operations cheaper, faster and easier to deploy across language barriers. But it still cannot fully replicate the cultural knowledge and lived experience embedded in a society.
Japan therefore does not need to build a wall capable of blocking every piece of false information. It needs to build an information environment in which foreign influence operations are less likely to succeed. As Japan and Taiwan confront increasingly similar information-security threats, sharing their experience in identifying and countering Chinese influence operations could become an increasingly important part of regional security cooperation.

articles.title: How Taiwan Became Singapore’s Largest Trading Partner
articles.full_text:
Economic ties are increasingly important, but Singapore cannot, and will not, become a defender of Taiwan’s international status.
In 2025, Taiwan overtook China as Singapore’s largest merchandise trading partner for the first time. According to Singapore’s Ministry of Trade and Industry, bilateral trade reached approximately S$170.3 billion (US$134 billion), ahead of Singapore’s trade with China (S$162.9 billion) and Malaysia (S$145.0 billion). One year earlier, Taiwan had ranked fourth. 
Singapore values Taiwan as a node in a diversified economic portfolio, but official diplomacy remains limited within the One China framework and Singapore has no incentive to revisit it.
Much of the bilateral trade between Singapore and Taiwan involves the semiconductor industry. Both Taiwan and Singapore have heavily invested in their AI industries to take advantage of the global AI boom. Taiwan’s semiconductor industry accounts for over 60 percent of global foundry revenue and more than 90 percent of leading-edge chip manufacturing, while Singapore has built out its AI ecosystem to include public research, public service adoption, and diffusion into commerce and industry. 
In 2025, roughly 80 percent of Taiwan’s exports to Singapore were semiconductors and related products, while about 60 percent of Singapore’s exports to Taiwan consisted of semiconductor equipment and intermediate goods. The surge in trade runs both ways. Singapore’s non-oil domestic exports to Taiwan last year grew 37.4 percent – the strongest performance among its major trading partners. 
As both economies occupy different stages in the AI supply chain, they have formed a highly complementary and closely linked cooperative network in Asia’s AI industry chain. Taiwan fabricates the overwhelming share of the world’s leading-edge logic chips through TSMC and its foundry ecosystem. Meanwhile, Singapore supplies equipment, materials, assembly, advanced packaging, and test capacity, and operates as the regional logistics and headquarters hub through which chips and inputs circulate. 
Both parties have also implemented national AI strategies that will end up strengthening this complementarity. Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong recently established a National AI Council alongside a series of national AI missions in advanced manufacturing, financial services, connectivity, and healthcare. Singapore also unveiled the world’s first governance framework for agentic AI at the World Economic Forum in January 2026, positioning itself as a standards-setter in AI. 
Concurrently, Taiwan has developed a Ten AI Initiatives Promotion Plan, an interagency effort that channels funding into silicon photonics, quantum technology, and AI robotics while building the infrastructure, talent, and capital to make Taiwan a “smart technology island.” Each set of measures raises domestic demand for end-use AI and embeds it in existing business models, feeding a cycle of rising demand and supply across both economies.
However, trade would never have scaled this quickly if the foundation hadn’t been laid years in advance. Under the agreement between Singapore and the Separate Customs Territory of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen and Matsu on Economic Partnership (ASTEP), signed in November 2013, Singapore eliminated tariffs on all Taiwanese imports, while Taiwan phased out duties on nearly all Singaporean goods, including electronics, machinery, and chemicals. ASTEP also streamlined customs and rules of origin for electronics, protected covered investments against forced technology transfer and local-content requirements, and enabled digitally supplied services without requiring a local office. 
Meanwhile, Taiwan’s New Southbound Strategy, implemented under former President Tsai Ing-wen’s administration, leveraged Singapore as a regional platform for Taiwanese investment and technology to expand into ASEAN and South Asian markets.
In addition to technological partnership, two-way financial flows between Taiwan and Singapore have shown significant increase. Taiwan’s economy grew 8.7 percent in 2025, its fastest rate in 15 years, and the Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Stock Index (TAIEX) more than doubled to a total market capitalization of US$4.4 trillion. The combined wealth of Taiwan’s 50 richest individuals rose 56 percent in a single year to a record US$308 billion, up from US$197 billion. KPMG Taiwan and E.Sun Bank project Taiwan’s high-net-worth population at 124,000 in 2026, holding combined assets of NT$46.1 trillion (US$1.47 trillion).
Much of that capital is being invested abroad. Hong Kong, once the default for Taiwanese wealth, has lost its appeal as Beijing has tightened political control. Now Singapore is taking Hong Kong’s place in Taiwanese investment portfolios. More than 80 percent of Taiwanese offshore assets were once concentrated in Hong Kong, but today 60-70 percent are managed in Singapore, amounting to roughly US$326 billion. Singapore’s combination of political stability, low tax rate, mature private banking systems, and accessible residency pathways has made it the preferred alternative. 
In addition, Singapore ranked as the largest foreign investor in Taiwan from January to July in 2026 with US$8.66 billion, accounting for 62.2 percent of inward Foreign Direct Investment during the period.  
While this unprecedented rise in trade owes in part to favorable economic tailwinds, it also reflects how both governments are managing national security and vulnerability in a region increasingly organized around geopolitical and technological competition. 
For Singapore, the relationship fits into its broader strategy of economic diversification, even as it rejects the idea of taking sides. Singapore has consistently resisted pressure to frame its choices as being either pro-American or pro-Chinese. Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan described the objective as remaining “relevant” and “useful” to multiple partners, maintaining Singapore’s “strategic choice” and “strategic autonomy.” 
Deeper economic ties with Taiwan can therefore be understood within that framework. Singapore wants to participate in the AI economy through relationships that span Taiwan, China, the United States, Europe, Japan, and Southeast Asia rather than depending on a single technology bloc. Taiwan’s value to Singapore is that it serves as another high-value economic partner, particularly in a sector that will shape future economic and military power. 
Increased trade with Taiwan, however, doesn’t mean that Singapore is tilting away from Beijing. China is still Singapore’s second-largest merchandise trading partner, and the two maintain extensive political ties. Moreover, Beijing has generally tolerated Singapore’s substantive unofficial ties with Taiwan when they remain consistent with Singapore’s One China policy, only objecting when interactions appear to carry greater political symbolism. 
For Taiwan, maintaining key economic relationships remains important in preserving its relevance to the world. Under President Lai Ching-te’s administration, “active diplomacy” and economic “indispensability” are two pillars of an emerging Taiwanese grand strategy. By embedding Taiwan more deeply in its partners’ technology ecosystems, Taipei gives foreign governments and firms a material stake in its continued autonomy and cross-strait stability. 
Singapore therefore matters not simply as a buyer of high-end Taiwanese products, but as a regional financial, logistics, and manufacturing hub through which Taiwanese firms can extend their reach and remain central to Asia’s AI economy.
Nonetheless, Taiwan should not expect the diplomatic status quo to change. Singapore maintains firm support for the One China policy at the highest level. In October 2025, following a meeting with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, Wong’s office stated that Singapore “has a clear and consistent ‘One China’ policy and is opposed to Taiwan independence.” In January 2026, Senior Minister (and former prime minister) Lee Hsien Loong restated the same formula at the Regional Outlook Forum, saying that Singapore upholds the One China Policy and is “against Taiwan independence” and “against unilateral changes to the status quo.”
Showing the complexity of the relationship, even while trade booms, Taiwan and Singapore’s security relationship has been eroding. Project Starlight is a military training program established in 1975 under an agreement between Lee Kuan Yew and Chiang Ching-kuo that permitted Singaporean troops to train annually in Taiwan. This has historically been an open secret that both parties have kept low profile to avoid Beijing’s protest. However, since the Terrex seizure incident in 2016, in which Hong Kong customs impounded Singaporean infantry carrier vehicles that were to transit to Taiwan, the scale of the training has dropped to roughly 3,000 people. 
When Taiwanese media publicized details of Starlight exercises in Pingtung in May 2026, Nikkei Asia reported that the disclosure may itself have been a signal timed ahead of the meeting between the U.S. and Chinese presidents to convey wariness about any China-U.S. bargain struck over Taiwan’s head. Therefore, Singapore-Taiwan security cooperation now reads more as a bargaining chip than as a commitment, and could be a strain to Singapore-Taiwan ties writ large.
Singapore has traditionally been a trusted party to both Taiwan and China because it has deep commercial and cultural ties with both parties, and because it has never formally endorsed Taiwan’s sovereign status, which is a non-negotiable for Beijing. Singapore has used that position to cultivate the role of a trusted intermediary. It hosted the 1993 Wang-Koo talks, the first semi-official cross-strait negotiations, and the 2015 Ma-Xi meeting, the first encounter between leaders on the two sides of the Taiwan Strait since 1949. 
Singapore’s neutrality provides a third-party venue for cross-strait contacts, which raises Singapore’s international reputation as an honest broker. But this neutrality will face increasing pressure as cross-strait relations worsen.
The Singapore-Taiwan relationship is primarily economic and financial; Singapore cannot, and will not, become a defender of Taiwan’s international status. Despite that limitation, Taiwan’s rise to the top of Singapore’s trade ledger is real and durable. Taipei should continue concentrating on the areas where returns are tangible: semiconductor supply chain integration, trade, capital markets, and talent flows. It should not, however, treat Singapore as a latent diplomatic partner or a candidate for public statements of support.

articles.title: Tarun Tejpal’s Conviction and India’s Discussions About the ‘Perfect Rape Victim’
articles.full_text:
It has also reignited debates around the role of the liberal media when the accused is one of their own.
A 2021 photograph of Tarun Tejpal, founder editor of Tehelka magazine, who was convicted on rape charges in August 2026.
She wore the wrong clothes. She was out at the wrong hours. She went to the wrong place. She is always in the wrong company. She was drunk. She invited it.
There have been plenty of ways to dismiss a rape or sexual harassment survivor by simply blaming them. This is so commonplace that, in 2021, a district court in the western Indian state of Goa acquitted a prominent magazine editor, holding that the accuser did not look traumatized in the CCTV footage captured moments after the incident.
Recently, a high court overturned the verdict, specifically dismissing the approach of scrutinizing how the survivor behaved.
The high-profile case involves Tarun Tejpal, who was the editor of the investigative news magazine Tehelka. A female junior colleague accused him of rape in 2013. In the August 2026 judgement, the Bombay High Court sentenced Tejpal to 10 years’ imprisonment.
The high court’s reliance on evidence rather than survivor behavior has been strongly welcomed by gender rights and civil rights activists and a section of journalists. “I believe the High Court judgment is important not just because of the individual involved, but because it reinforces a larger principle,” wrote political commentator Sujit Nair.
Even in 2002, Indian laws allowed men accused of rape to show that the survivor was of generally immoral character. Section 155(4) of the Indian Evidence Act stated that “when a man is prosecuted for rape or an attempt to ravish, it may be shown that the prosecutrix was of generally immoral character.”
Way back in 1980, the Indian Law Commission had recommended that in a case of rape or attempted rape, any evidence or cross-examination related to the past immoral character of the survivor “should be prohibited except as regards sexual relations with the accused.” The commission held it was necessary to “exclude the possibility of evidence of general immoral character being tendered.”
While Section 155(4) was finally deleted in 2003, the government did not impose the explicit prohibition in such questioning as suggested by the commission. This loophole was subsequently exploited, journalist and author Manoj Mitta wrote in a recent article. “The prohibition only on the questions about her character proved insufficient to save her from interrogation about her sex life,” Mitta wrote.
The loophole was finally blocked when India rewrote its anti-rape law in the aftermath of the 2012 gang-rape of a medical student in a moving bus in the national capital of New Delhi. The new law also expanded the definition of rape — covering penetration of the vagina, anus, urethra, or mouth by any object or any part of the body, not just the penis.
The Tarun Tejpal case was the first high-profile case filed soon after the new law came into effect. And yet, during the trial, the survivor faced the same harrowing questions about her behavior after the alleged incident.
The lower court judgement showed it relied on the survivor’s behavior, which it thought did not match that of a raped woman. The survivor’s conduct “neither demonstrates any kind of normative behavior on her own part that a prosecutrix of sexual assault on consecutive two nights might plausibly show, nor does it demonstrate any such behavior on the part of the accused,” said the 2021 judgement.
While hearing the appeal against the judgement, a Bombay High Court judge had even commented that the lower court judgement “seems like a manual for rape victims,” criticizing how much space it devoted to prescribing appropriate survivor behavior.
After the recent verdict, the survivor broke her silence for the first time in 13 years. In a Substack essay, she wrote that she knew only the truth of her body, “frozen with fear, sexually assaulted by a man nearly twice my age, a man responsible for my livelihood, a man who my father knew and trusted, whose family I was close to.”
She explicitly mentioned how the “good victim vs bad victim” battle exhausted her: “My past became a way to deny, and worse, justify my assault: My relationships, my financial precarity, my loneliness, my clumsiness as a 20-something woman figuring her way as a young adult in a new city with new friends. Even my professionalism became a cudgel in the hands of male rage.”
But it’s not only “male rage” that she speaks about. She also mentions how she faced questions on her motivation in accusing a “supposed ‘liberal’ ‘hero’ of rape.”
This is where the second aspect of the Tejpal controversy comes up — the role of the liberal media and the liberal intelligentsia in handling cases where one of their own is involved.
The incident took place inside a hotel elevator in 2013 during an event organized by the magazine in Goa. Tejpal had initially written  to the survivor, saying, “I apologize unconditionally for the shameful lapse of judgement that led me to attempt a sexual liaison with you on two occasions…. despite your clear reluctance.” However, later he called himself a victim of a political conspiracy.
Tejpal had become a big name in Indian journalism. A sting operation he led in 2001 had severely hurt the Bharatiya Janata Party government under then-Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee. He had earned accolades like “powerful and pioneering,” “one of Asia’s 50 most powerful communicators,” among “50 leaders at the forefront of change in Asia,” and India’s “most feted journalist.”
In 2013, when the controversy broke out, Goa was under the BJP, the party which bore the brunt of Tehelka’s 2001 sting operation. Therefore, Tejpal alleged a political vendetta behind the allegations.
During the subsequent months, several liberals voiced support for Tejpal. Tehelka managing editor Shoma Choudhury was accused of trying to shield Tejpal. In 2014, the news magazine Outlook carried a cover story in which journalist and best-selling author Manu Joseph wrote a highly controversial piece dissecting the behavior of the survivor from CCTV footage he managed to access. The piece, which was highly sympathetic toward Tejpal, quoted him as saying: “She may not have intended to but what she has done is that she has delivered me to the right wing. That’s what she has done.”
In the words of journalist Ranjona Banerji, “Tragically, as in so many cases, the bulk of the old media ganged up against young women journalists for daring to have a voice.”
Even after the recent high court conviction, documentary filmmaker Anand Patwardhan, a prominent face in India’s left-liberal intelligentsia circuit, expressed his suspicion that the high court verdict was possibly a way of pleasing India’s ruling party, the BJP.
“Tejpal preying on young colleagues is reprehensible,” Patwardhan commented on a social media post, adding, “Was it rape?” He then said the CCTV footage of Tejpal and the survivor “entering the lift as well as exiting from it on the upper floor, talking normally” leads him to conclude that no violent incident happened in the lift itself.
When a leading left-liberal voice invests in investigating survivor body language, it does not speak well of those who hold their likes in high esteem.
In her essay, Banerji had asked, “Is rape therefore tolerable if the assaulter is a liberal?” Perhaps this is a question that the high priests of accountability and public-spirited journalism need to ask themselves more deeply. The time has arrived — no matter how the Supreme Court deals with Tejpal’s appeal against the Bombay High Court judgment.

articles.title: The South China Sea and the Philippines’ Defense Strategies
articles.full_text:
Insights from Su Mon and Tomas Buenaventura.
A photo released by the Armed Forces of the Philippines that claims to show a China Coast Guard vessel firing a water cannon in the vicinity of Second Thomas Shoal in the South China Sea, Aug. 20, 2025.
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Su Mon and Tomas Buenaventura – Asia Pacific senior analyst and senior research assistant, respectively, at ACLED (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data) – is the 523rd in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”
Examine the South China Sea conflict escalation environment based on ACLED data.
ACLED data reveals the South China Sea security environment is increasingly defined by the normalization of gray zone tactics and rapid militarization. A persistent state of confrontation significantly escalated in the first half of 2026, with a roughly 490 percent increase in Chinese force movements between January and June compared to the previous six months. This activity is concentrated within the Philippines’ Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), specifically around Scarborough Shoal, Sabina Shoal, and Thitu Island.
This uptick in force movements — including survey vessels, China Coast Guard (CCG) deployments, and maritime militia — is often accompanied by more frequent encounters, ranging from harassment and blocking maneuvers to competing law enforcement operations. These activities are not just about presence, but about altering the status quo on the seas. They represent a coordinated effort to advance territorial claims and consolidate control, keeping tensions high while strategically averting open military conflict. 
Essentially, the region has become a primary theater for power projection, where the margin for error is shrinking, and the risks of a miscalculation that could lead to broader instability are becoming more acute.
How are gray zone tactics affecting the chance of escalation in the South China Sea?
The real danger with gray zone operations is not necessarily that they will spark an immediate war; it’s that they gradually normalize coercion. By using persistent, incremental actions — such as the routine deployment of maritime militia and coast guard vessels — Beijing is steadily shifting the status quo, redefining “normal” maritime activity in a way that feels manageable daily but creates significant long-term strategic shifts.
ACLED’s South China Sea Monitor suggests that these gray zone operations are expanding into cyber warfare, intelligence operations, and suspected sabotage against critical infrastructure. This expansion shows the growing imbalance between China and other claimant states, necessitating stronger cooperation among regional partners and allies to respond effectively.
Ultimately, this creates a dangerous environment where the primary risk is not a deliberate decision to go to war, but a miscalculation. As these tactics become more sophisticated, they blur strategic intent and erode the trust needed to manage crises. Regional security and coordination mechanisms, such as the South China Sea Code of Conduct negotiations, have not kept pace with these developments, leaving a widening gap in governance, making the region increasingly vulnerable to unintended escalations.
Identify key developments in the Scarborough Shoal and the Spratly Islands.
The situation at Scarborough Shoal has remained tense since China established de facto control there in 2012, despite the feature falling within the Philippines’ EEZ. Beijing has maintained a constant presence, with the CCG and maritime militia frequently blocking, ramming, and using water cannons against Philippine vessels. Tensions intensified after Beijing designated the shoal a national “nature reserve” in September 2025 — a move China framed as environmental protection, but which Manila viewed as an attempt to consolidate administrative control. Subsequent reports of floating barriers, buoys, and a temporary research platform further heightened tensions, culminating in confrontations on July 23-24, 2026, when the CCG again deployed water cannons against Philippine government vessels.
The Spratly Islands present a more complex, multilayered security environment involving competing claims from Brunei, China, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan, and Vietnam. The challenge here is twofold: immediate flashpoints and gradual, strategic military expansion. Second Thomas Shoal remains one of the most volatile flashpoints. While an informal arrangement since mid-2024 has reduced interference with routine Philippine resupply missions to the BRP Sierra Madre, China continues to block construction materials intended to strengthen the outpost. The recent clash on July 22 at Second Thomas demonstrates that both sides are contending over what constitutes acceptable military presence. 
Developments at Scarborough Shoal and the Spratly Islands reflect a broader contest, as China and the Philippines test resolve and respond to perceived encroachments. Each side is enforcing its own red lines, but in doing so is edging closer to crossing the other’s.
Analyze how the United States-Philippines Mutual Defense Treaty (MDT) could draw Washington into a broader regional conflict. 
The Mutual Defense Treaty (MDT) signed by Manila and Washington in 1951 obligates both countries to come to each other’s defense in case of an armed attack on either in the Pacific region. As the treaty’s scope explicitly identified armed attacks as the trigger to both sides’ defense obligations, this has given rise to the widespread use of “gray zone” tactics on China’s part in its assertion of its maritime territorial claims against the Philippines. This seemingly hard limit for China’s South China Sea activity allows Beijing to pressure Manila on its claims while keeping the risk of armed conflict with the U.S. at bay. Still, the very nature of gray zone tactics at sea — consisting of close vessel confrontations, tailing and blocking actions, and other delicate maneuvers — means that the risk of a lethal accident is never zero. 
Already, this July, a widely publicized confrontation between Chinese and Philippine personnel near Second Thomas Shoal left a Philippine soldier injured after being struck with a wooden baton. Even in this high-profile incident, though, no side has risked employing any sort of actual firepower against each other, as that would be indisputably escalatory and definitely be a notch above the confrontations of recent years — and likely enough reason for the U.S. to consider a heightened presence in the waters. 
Assess the current gray zone conditions between the Philippines and China. 
Despite the heated rhetoric between Manila and Beijing, the Philippines and China continue to engage each other very closely through diplomatic channels. Nevertheless, the tense environment created by the constant gray zone operations provides a conducive environment for potential triggers to MDT defense obligations, say, a lethal incident that leads both Chinese and Philippine forces to reach for firepower. In such a situation, the Philippines would count on the U.S. to make good on its repeated affirmations of its “ironclad” commitment to the Philippines’ defense. 
For the time being, however, neither the Philippines and China seem to have any real desire to engage each other in armed conflict, especially given the otherwise close economic ties between the two countries. Thus, as long as the gray zone activities are managed to a tolerable degree, no matter how feisty the rhetoric gets between Manila and Beijing, they are currently unlikely to draw the U.S. into a conflict in the region.

articles.title: The Iran War Is Disrupting Trade Connectivity Across Eurasia
articles.full_text:
Central Asia aims to benefit from Iranian ports and railroads have been disrupted by the ongoing conflict.
There are no current or planned ceasefire negotiations between Iran and the United States. U.S. President Donald Trump called for an “economic D-Day” against Iran on August 19; when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent fleshed that threat out on August 24, the announcement consisted of a warning shot rather than any new immediate penalties. 
Until another ceasefire is agreed upon by both sides, global trade routes through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea are clouded with risk. But existing trade routes are not the only ones impacted by the conflict. The war in Iran is also holding hostage the future of trade and connectivity across the wider Eurasian continent. 
On July 8, after the previous ceasefire fell apart, U.S. forces launched missile strikes against multiple targets in Iran. In one instance, Financial Times reported cruise missiles struck and visibly damaged the Agh Tekeh Khan (also spelled “Aq Tekeh Khan”) railway bridge near the city of Aqqala in northern Iran. While several bridges and railways were targeted, this is one of only two railroads that lead out of Iran into Turkmenistan. It connects two separate railroads: the Iran-Turkmenistan-Kazakhstan Railway and the eastern route of the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC). 
According to a report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), India, Iran, and Russia agreed to the construction of the INSTC in September 2000, with many more countries, including Kazakhstan and Tajikistan, joining before the end of the decade. Another initiative, the European Union-financed Transport Corridor Europe-Caucasus- Asia (TRACECA) program, was formed in Belgium in 1993 to develop a transport corridor linking Europe to Central Asia. Iran joined as a member in June 2009. Two years later Iran, Oman, Qatar, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan signed the Ashgabat Agreement, to increase and simplify transportation and trade across the region. Qatar withdrew in 2013, but Kazakhstan, Pakistan, and India signed on in recent years. 
Many of these countries have invested resources into expanding railways across the region, especially in Iran with its rail lines stretching from Turkmenistan to ports along the Persian Gulf and Arabian Sea. For landlocked countries like Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, access to the ports of Bandar Abbas and Chabahar are opportunities to trade more easily across oceans. 
On June 28, Iran and Kazakhstan signed an agreement allowing the latter to build and operate a terminal at Shahid Rajaee Port near the city and port of Bandar Abbas. The 27-year agreement, with two years to build and 25 years to operate, allocates 15 hectares of space at the Iranian port, with Kazakhstan providing privately sourced investment funds for its construction. The two railway corridors passing through Kazakhstan to the coast of Iran means that Kazakhstan will see the benefits of the project relatively quickly.
The only Iranian port sitting on the Arabian Sea, the port of Chabahar, is a lucrative location for Uzbekistan by providing access to the ocean. Uzbekistan signed an agreement with Iran in 2022 to construct infrastructure facilities at the port. This would establish a trade route from India’s ports to Chabahar and send goods by rail through Iran and Turkmenistan. Compared to Uzbekistan’s agreement with Iran to develop a logistics center in Bandar Abbas, the port of Chabahar is a closer and more secure route to India.
India has invested hundreds of millions of dollars to develop the port of Chabahar since 2015. The port’s location allows India to bypass China and Pakistan and would be unaffected by future closures of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf. Amid China’s pledge to invest $62 billion on connectivity with Pakistan, particularly the port of Gwadar, India’s presence at Chabahar is a both political move and a trade opportunity. India and Iran signed a $370 million, 10-year deal in 2024 to allow the former to operate at the port. 
Iran and Pakistan have made multiple agreements to improve connectivity with one another’s highways. Al Jazeera reported in April that Pakistan issued an order allowing for shipments from third parties unable to reach Iranian ports to pass through its ports and arrive in Iran overland. The quickest route, from the port of Gwadar to Gabd at the Iranian border, takes 2-3 hours. The continuation of the war shows how Pakistan can act as an alternate route when Iran’s ports are closed off.  
When the United States resumed attacks in early July, Iran’s railways and ports were hit hard, damaging the Agh Tekeh Khan railway bridge, multiple bridges, and a tunnel near the port of Bandar Abbas, and key infrastructure, including a maritime traffic control tower, at the port of Chabahar. 
Although the site for the Kazakh terminal at Bandar Abbas Port was not damaged, Kazakhstan’s government is delaying its construction. Before the war, Uzbekistan paused plans to establish its own presence at Chabahar. Now the war is forcing Uzbekistan to hold off on the plan indefinitely. 
The Trump administration’s heavy sanctions against the port and its refusal to grant another sanctions exemption waiver raised concerns in India regarding Chabahar’s safety. According to an April article from Bloomberg, India was considering handing control of its section of the port back to Iran before the waiver expiration.
The war in Iran has forced the Central Asian states and India to look for alternate routes. Last July, Uzbekistan signed a trilateral agreement on a feasibility study for the Uzbekistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan Trans-Afghan Railway Project. The Tashkent Times reported in June that the feasibility study is expected to be completed by the end of the year.
Pakistani representatives talked with Kazakh delegates at the end of July about opening terminals in Pakistan’s ports at Karachi, Qasim, and Gwadar. A transport corridor through Afghanistan into Pakistan would allow Central Asian states to bypass Iran and connect to more stable ports. This route suggests that Iran is at risk of losing its Central Asian and Indian customers. 
However, the war itself does not make Iranian ports or railways less valuable for trade. The routes through Iran are faster and cheaper than shipping goods through the Black Sea, the Suez Canal, the Red Sea, and around the Arabian Peninsula. As Fatemah Aman wrote in The National Interest, “the conflict has not erased these advantages.” 
The Trans-Afghan Corridor would be geographically insulated from future Iranian instability, though not from any future instability in Afghanistan. It would reach Pakistan quickly, but its construction has not begun. The corridor is estimated to cost between $4.6 billion and $7 billion and will take at least five years to complete. While the corridor through Afghanistan is decoupled from the risks associated with the Iran war, it is a future solution instead of a present one and burdened by its own set of risks, not the least of which is the tense Afghanistan-Pakistan relationship.
The biggest concern overshadowing the projects with the ports and railroads in Iran is the likelihood of them being attacked. At a time when the Trump administration is pursuing greater cooperation with Central and South Asia, U.S. strikes and economic warcraft pose the greatest risk to these initiatives. The United States has not only further destabilized the Middle East, but it is also disrupting multiple Eurasian trade plans that have been in the works for decades.

articles.title: JASDF Fighter Jets to Visit India for First Time
articles.full_text:
Three F-2A fighters will fly to India via Okinawa and Thailand for Veer Guardian 26, with the U.S. Air Force providing support including aerial refueling.
A Japan Air Self-Defense Force F-2A fighter aircraft. Three F-2As are scheduled to deploy to India in September for Veer Guardian 26.
The Japan Air Self-Defense Force (JASDF) will send fighter aircraft to India for the first time in September to participate in a bilateral exercise with the Indian Air Force (IAF), marking another milestone in the deepening defense partnership between Tokyo and New Delhi.
The JASDF announced on August 25 that the bilateral exercise, Veer Guardian 26, will take place from September 9 to 21 at Jodhpur Air Force Station in the northwestern Indian state of Rajasthan and in surrounding airspace. The overall deployment period, including the journey to and from India, will run from September 1 to 30. 
The JASDF will deploy three F-2A fighters from the 8th Air Wing at Tsuiki Air Base in Fukuoka Prefecture, southwestern Japan, along with about 110 personnel. The exercise will primarily involve air combat training against fighter aircraft.
On August 26, a JASDF spokesman told The Diplomat that Veer Guardian 26 will be the second iteration of the bilateral fighter exercise, following the inaugural Veer Guardian 23 held in Japan in January 2023.
During that exercise, the IAF sent four Su-30MKI fighters, two C-17 transport aircraft, an IL-78 aerial refueling tanker, and about 150 personnel to Japan. The JASDF participated with four F-2 and four F-15 fighters. 
Three years later, the direction of travel will be reversed, with JASDF fighters heading to India for the first time.
The journey to India is itself a significant part of the deployment. The JASDF spokesman told The Diplomat that the three F-2As will fly from Tsuiki Air Base to Jodhpur via Naha Air Base in Okinawa and Thailand. The U.S. Air Force will provide support for the deployment, including aerial refueling.
The JASDF did not disclose the specific base in Thailand where the F-2As will stop, the segment of the journey during which U.S. aerial refueling support will be provided, or the type of U.S. tanker aircraft involved.
Jodhpur lies roughly 5,600 kilometers from Tsuiki in a straight line, underscoring the logistical challenge of deploying a fighter unit far beyond Japan.
Speaking at a press conference at Japan’s Ministry of Defense in Tokyo on August 25, JASDF Chief of Staff General Morita Takehiro emphasized the operational significance of such a long-range deployment.
The JASDF’s top officer said deploying fighters to distant locations involves not only long-distance flight operations but also maintenance, logistics, and personnel transportation, all of which must be conducted “in an integrated and systematic manner.” Such experience, he said, helps improve a unit’s ability to carry out its missions.
Long-distance deployments also require the JASDF to prepare for contingencies such as bad weather and aircraft malfunctions.
Drawing on lessons and knowledge gained from previous overseas deployments, Morita said the JASDF is preparing for the India mission by securing spare aircraft, strengthening its aerial refueling support system, reviewing transit locations, and closely coordinating with relevant countries.
The deployment to India follows the JASDF’s first fighter deployment to Europe in 2025. During that mission, four F-15 fighters flew from Chitose Air Base in Hokkaido to the United Kingdom and Germany via Eielson Air Force Base in Alaska and Canadian Forces Base Goose Bay, supported by tanker and transport aircraft. The JASDF described that deployment as an opportunity to strengthen cooperation with allies and like-minded countries.
Veer Guardian 26 comes as both Japan and India face growing security challenges involving China. Japan has become increasingly concerned not only about Chinese military activities in the East China Sea and around its southwestern islands, but also about the People’s Liberation Army’s expanding operations beyond the First Island Chain and farther into the Western Pacific. India, meanwhile, has a long-running territorial dispute with China along their Himalayan border.
However, when asked by The Diplomat whether Veer Guardian 26 was being conducted with China in mind, the spokesman at the JASDF said the exercise “is not aimed at any specific country.”
Whatever the motivation, Japan and India are deepening their overall defense ties. Japanese Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro and Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh met in New Delhi on August 20 and welcomed progress in preparations for Veer Guardian 26, specifically noting that JASDF fighters would visit India for the first time. 
The two ministers also agreed to deepen bilateral exercise cooperation by increasing the complexity of drills, integrating unmanned systems, and pursuing short-notice joint exercises when opportunities arise. They highlighted the expansion of exercises across all three services, including the army exercise Dharma Guardian and the maritime exercise JAIMEX. 
The meeting also saw the signing of a memorandum on maritime security cooperation, while both sides reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening defense cooperation in pursuit of a “free and open Indo-Pacific.” 
For the JASDF, the first deployment of F-2As to India therefore has significance beyond the bilateral exercise itself. It will deepen tactical cooperation and mutual understanding with the Indian Air Force while giving the JASDF another opportunity, following last year’s European deployment, to hone its ability to deploy fighter units far from Japan, again with support from the U.S. Air Force.
The Japan Air Self-Defense Force (JASDF) will send fighter aircraft to India for the first time in September to participate in a bilateral exercise with the Indian Air Force (IAF), marking another milestone in the deepening defense partnership between Tokyo and New Delhi.
The JASDF announced on August 25 that the bilateral exercise, Veer Guardian 26, will take place from September 9 to 21 at Jodhpur Air Force Station in the northwestern Indian state of Rajasthan and in surrounding airspace. The overall deployment period, including the journey to and from India, will run from September 1 to 30. 
The JASDF will deploy three F-2A fighters from the 8th Air Wing at Tsuiki Air Base in Fukuoka Prefecture, southwestern Japan, along with about 110 personnel. The exercise will primarily involve air combat training against fighter aircraft.
On August 26, a JASDF spokesman told The Diplomat that Veer Guardian 26 will be the second iteration of the bilateral fighter exercise, following the inaugural Veer Guardian 23 held in Japan in January 2023.
During that exercise, the IAF sent four Su-30MKI fighters, two C-17 transport aircraft, an IL-78 aerial refueling tanker, and about 150 personnel to Japan. The JASDF participated with four F-2 and four F-15 fighters. 
Three years later, the direction of travel will be reversed, with JASDF fighters heading to India for the first time.
The journey to India is itself a significant part of the deployment. The JASDF spokesman told The Diplomat that the three F-2As will fly from Tsuiki Air Base to Jodhpur via Naha Air Base in Okinawa and Thailand. The U.S. Air Force will provide support for the deployment, including aerial refueling.
The JASDF did not disclose the specific base in Thailand where the F-2As will stop, the segment of the journey during which U.S. aerial refueling support will be provided, or the type of U.S. tanker aircraft involved.
articles.summary: Three F-2A fighters will fly to India via Okinawa and Thailand for Veer Guardian 26, with the U.S. Air Force providing support including aerial refueling.

articles.title: Pakistan’s Kashmir Crackdown
articles.full_text:
A “sham” election sparked popular outrage in nominally autonomous Pakistan-administered Kashmir – and a corresponding security crackdown.
The Madina Market of Muzaffarabad, a major regional commercial hub, has finally reopened to economic activity following weeks of turmoil. Muzaffarabad – the capital of Pakistan-administered Kashmir, housing the Prime Minister’s Secretariat, the Legislative Assembly, and other government buildings emblematic of its on-paper autonomy – is showing signs of a return to daily life. Likewise, Mirpur, the region’s second largest city, has now resumed intracity public transportation, allowing locals to move between Pakistan and the territory Islamabad dubs as Azad, or Free Jammu and Kashmir. Nevertheless, Pakistan-administered Kashmir still has a visibly heightened deployment of security personnel.
Over the past three months, at least 80 people have been killed across the region amid the general election in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, which was held from July 27 to August 10. The election, which was widely deemed contentious owing to allegations of polling day irregularities, in addition to pre-election machinations alleged to benefit status quo parties, saw the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and Pakistan People’s Party (PPP) – which are also leading the ruling alliance in Islamabad – emerge victorious.
“The elections were a sham. No one who actually wants any betterment for the locals participated in the election. It is not an election when all the votes go to one party: the Pakistan army,” Tariq Rehman, a schoolteacher in Kotli, told The Diplomat.
Pakistan’s omnipotent military establishment has maintained arbitrary control over the region since the 1947 partition of the Indian subcontinent divided the erstwhile state of Jammu and Kashmir between India and Pakistan. Both states administer part of Jammu and Kashmir but claim the territory in its entirety, and they have fought multiple wars over it. 
In August 2019, India revoked Article 370 of its constitution, which undid the special status of Indian-administered Kashmir. Since then, multiple Pakistani government sources, including military officials, have told The Diplomat that there have been plans to mainstream the Pakistani-administered Kashmir, effectively upholding the Line of Control dividing the territory as an international border. Calls to divide Pakistan’s existing provinces have also gathered pace in recent months.
While the Pakistani state makes up its mind over the status of its controlled section of Kashmir, the locals have been stuck in limbo, unsure of their relationship with the country. Whether they are a distinct autonomous region – as upheld by Pakistan’s longstanding position and internationalization of the Kashmir dispute – or just a part of Pakistan is a question that has manifested in local political, social, and cultural expressions.   
“They want us to be Pakistanis when they feel like it. They want us to be Kashmiris when they feel like it. But the recent bloodshed shows that they want us to remain captives to their power games. Who kills people for demanding that we should have a say in deciding our own future?” said Mir Hamza, a Muzaffarabad-based artisan, who had participated in recent protests and was witness to security personnel firing on protestors. “My brother [cousin] is still in Rawalakot. We want to continue the movement until we can achieve our fundamental human rights.”
As the sit-in continues in Rawalakot, local authorities have made the city inaccessible, with media barred from reporting in the region. Internet blackouts have been in place to limit social media coverage, and laws have been passed requiring a No Objection Certificate (NOC) for coverage of any news. 
Many international and local publications have been blocked in Pakistan. One of them is the Urdu publication Daily Jeddojehad, which has documented the deaths in Pakistan-administered Kashmir amid the recent state crackdown. 
“Security agencies raided my home. In my absence, three of my family members were picked up. They told my family that my articles on Kashmir were anti-national and the raid was aimed at arresting me,” Jeddojehad editor Farooq Sulehria told The Diplomat. 
“I was in London, hence I was lucky to escape. However, I am not able to return to Pakistan,” he added.
Many journalists and activists have been summoned over dissent in Pakistan-administered Kashmir in order to enforce complete censorship. “This is unprecedented. The state wants to deny the people of Jammu and Kashmir the possibility to voice their protest on social media against the violent repression. It wants to disseminate one-dimensional information and propaganda,” Sulehria said.
These measures have been put in place as part of the crackdown on the local protesters, who have been galvanized in recent years by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC).
Since September 2023, the JAAC has rallied for the locals’ right to have control over their own resources, with the committee emphasizing issues ranging from power and commodity prices to governance reforms. As part of its list of demands, a major political reform sought by the JAAC was the undoing of seat reservations for muhajirs, or immigrants from Indian-administered Kashmir. As things stand, 12 of the 53 seats in the legislature of Pakistan-administered Kashmir are allocated to such individuals – who could be residing outside the territory. JAAC members and critics told The Diplomat that this arrangement not only reduces local representation, but also allows the military establishment to maintain its political stranglehold. 
“Azad Jammu & Kashmir should only be ruled by the people of Azad Jammu & Kashmir. Not those in uniform, nor their selected parties, nor those being picked for the reserved seats to toe the lines of the powers that be,” JAAC core leader Shaukat Nawaz Mir had told The Diplomat when the latest protests erupted in June. 
Mir, among other JAAC members, has since been detained. The government slapped sedition charges on them following the announcement of “head money” over information pertaining to these individuals. The JAAC has been declared a terrorist organization by the Pakistani state, with many of its activists either being detained or voluntarily going underground.
While the JAAC enjoys significant support among the people of Pakistan-administered Kashmir, it has its skeptics as well. “I don’t know who they are, and whom they are fighting for. Some say they are Indian agents. All I know is that because of the violence and the internet shutdown I have lost significant business and customers,” said Mohammed Iqbal, a Chakswari-based restaurant owner. 
According to Madina Market Traders Association President Raja Abrar Mustafa, most of the traders had supported the JAAC initially, but gradually the committee’s position hardened on some issues. “We have supported them over issues related to the public and economic issues. But traders shouldn’t get involved in constitutional matters,” he said. 
Many of the JAAC’s critics, new and old – including those who are a part of the government machinery – nonetheless concede that most of the demands the committee had brought to the table reflected the sentiments of the majority of the local population, even if some matters might have been contentious. 
“All of the committee’s demands were accepted. But they continued to fixate over one [on seat reservation], causing so much turmoil. What did all this achieve for the locals?” asked Mirpur-based PML-N leader Chaudhary Muhammad Saeed while talking to The Diplomat. 
Saeed, who lost his Mirpur seat in the recent elections, said while the voter turnout was lower – around 50 percent compared to the usual 60 percent – it wasn’t different enough to suggest a widespread clash between the locals and the state. “Yes, some people are unhappy over certain issues, and yes, some political reforms are needed in Azad Kashmir. But what is more pertinent are economic reforms. There would be no need for such protests where there is financial stability,” he said.
Even so, many of the people who are “unhappy” are unable to participate in these conversations, or respond to the ubiquitous state-sponsored criticism against them. Many of the state’s critics are in jail, in exile, or have disappeared.
