articles.title: The South Korean Government’s Housing Policy Tanks Its Approval Ratings
articles.full_text:
Even the historic Yongsan Park isn’t safe from the government’s desire for more housing.
A view of Yongsan Park, with the National Museum of Korea on the left.
Seoulites and tourists primarily associate Yongsan Park with the National Museum of Korea. Located in the middle of the southernmost strip of the park, it attracts the third highest number of annual visitors in the world.
Walking up to the front affords quite a sight. A lone pavilion, with its rooftop faded in jade green, stands in a tree-lined pond. Trace the gaze upward, and there’s the rectangular gap in the museum’s superstructure of concrete covered in granite framing the beautiful expanse of greenery opening up to Namsan Mountain and Namsan Tower. At the back of the premise is a children’s garden, filling the air around the museum with laughter and scampering footsteps.
This break from the city’s noise and visual fatigue is thanks to the fact that it used to be Yongsan Garrison. In 1953, the United States 8th Army moved into what is today Yongsan Park  – only a tiny portion is open to the public so far – to deter North Korea. In 1957, the United Nations Command also relocated next to the U.S. base from Tokyo. This 630-acre post, plus Itaewon just outside of the garrison, had become a little America in the heart of Seoul.
It remained untouched until 1989, when then-South Korean President Roh Tae-woo and U.S. President George H. W. Bush got into a chopper and circled over Yongsan Garrison. The view reportedly convinced Bush to agree that “there shouldn’t be foreign troops in the middle of a state’s capital.” 
The next year, Washington and Seoul signed an agreement to relocate the U.S. forces somewhere else. Successive South Korean governments then framed the matter of nudging U.S. soldiers out of Seoul as reviving national pride. After much dithering, it was finally decided in 2004 that Camp Humphreys, an hour drive south of Seoul, would absorb Yongsan forces. 
What would become of the newly vacated land in Seoul?
The Roh Moo-hyun administration legislated the 2007 Special Act on the Creation of Yongsan Park. The act bound the government to develop the land to be returned from the United States “into a place for leisure and relaxation as well as a natural and ecological space.” It also barred development of the area into anything other than a park.
However, the base territory has changed hands at a painfully slow pace. Although most U.S. personnel and military materiel vacated Yongsan to Camp Humphreys, Washington has coughed up only some 30 percent of the land. The handover of the rest awaits talks on recompensation, environmental inspections, and cleanup. 
But its fate is already generating controversy.
In mid-August, the Lee administration kicked up an intense public uproar with its controversial idea to build housing in the Yongsan complex. “Yongsan is so huge … There are places where I think we can build housing,” said the president’s economic development guru in a radio appearance. He then floated the idea of building apartment complexes in the children’s garden section of Yongsan Park. 
The land and infrastructure ministry followed up with its announcement that it would survey where to build new housing in the park, particularly those areas already razed to the ground by the U.S. military. 
This was all in response to President Lee Jae-myung’s exhortation to his aides on August 13 to “devote all available resources and capabilities to solving housing problems that threaten people’s livelihood and the state’s future.” Indeed, South Korea’s real estate investment and redevelopment frenzy has jacked up housing prices for decades. In a country where owning a flat is a prerequisite for marriage, this has been one of the many factors driving down birthrates. And the increasing inequality in wealth determined by real estate ownership isn’t a tenable social reality. 
So, the Lee administration has implemented a slew of policies meant to deter frenetic property purchases. Two of these particularly attracted opprobrium. First, shrinking the proportion of a loan homebuyers can secure out of the total property value has forced them to look to leases. Higher demand for leases led to higher rent and premiums (an upfront lump-sum payment for granting a lease). But now, there’s even a shortage of leases. 
Second, the government proposed increasing the cap on the real estate holding tax and the market valuation rates used to assess property value for tax purposes.
Together, these policies had the effect of alienating most Seoul residents, both tenants and homeowners. Polls in mid-August showed that Lee’s approval rating fell below the 50 percentage mark for the first time since his term began. The housing crisis and prosecutorial reform were cited as the two major reasons. Among young residents in Seoul, Lee’s performance was abysmal, at 31 percent.
There is no question that more affordable housing is needed, which is why the government pledged to lay the groundwork for about 1.5 million new publicly funded flats during Lee’s term. That’s also why the Lee administration bucked the liberal regimes’ historical stance against bulldozing greenbelts – and whether Yongsan Park should become part of this plan is now a raging debate.
The government’s urgency is understandable, but the park should be inviolable. Seoul needs a breathing space. The only silver lining in the U.S. Army’s use of the base was that it saved a huge chunk in the heart of Seoul from the city’s unrestrained development and construction before the concept of landscape urbanism –  that greenery and ecosystem should inform architectural plans – was even a thing in South Korea. Seoul needs something akin to New York’s Central Park and London’s Hyde Park and Regent’s Park. Yongsan Park, once Washington returns more plots, could be larger and play a vastly positive role. As the lungs of the city, the park could nurture precious ecology, dampen heat waves, and add social value as a shared natural space.
Also, Yongsan Park should be preserved and developed into a full-blown park for symbolic and historical reasons. The location represents the country’s painful history, independence, and modernity.
Empires of old dug in their heels here. In the 13th century, Mongols occupied the area for their war against Korea. In the 17th century, China’s Qing Dynasty quartered their soldiers here, from which they trafficked 5 percent of the Korean population. Throughout the first half of the 20th century, Imperial Japan’s soldiers sojourned here, conscripting and training and sending Koreans to their deaths in Japan’s far-flung wars. And then the United States took over the base in 1945. 
It has also been Korea’s gateway to the world. Owing to its centrality and proximity to the Han River and Namsan Mountain, foreign tourists and traders have converged here since medieval times. Goods crisscrossing the country passed through Yongsan’s barter shops and entry routes. Since the late 19th century, it was through here that Koreans introduced modernity, be it steamboats and trams, or multiculturalism and artistic development.
It is time now for South Koreans to savor this space. It should not be turned into apartment complexes. 
The Lee administration said that the vast majority of the park will be spared. But apartment complexes mean auxiliary infrastructure. Roads have to be laid down. Malls and schools have to be built. Carving the park this way ruins the last precious chance to rectify Seoul’s cramped landscape and restore biological diversity.
Seoul’s mayor Oh Se-hoon is locking horns with the government over this issue. 
“History won’t forgive me for allowing even a small portion of the park to be turned into apartment sites,” Oh said in a video he filmed at the park. “We need to preserve Yongsan’s history and nature for the future generations,” he added. 
He’s not alone. The most recent survey released on August 24 found that two out of three Seoulites are against the government proposal. The Seoul Metropolitan Government has been holding a series of talks with the government to persuade the latter of alternatives.
It’s worth remembering that in 2016, the Park Geun-hye administration wanted to build a couple of museums in the park. It was pelted with public outrage for even broaching the idea of pouring concrete in this historical land. The government backed down.
What Seoul needs isn’t traditional housing reconstruction and redevelopment practices, still less marring Yongsan Park for drab, high-rise apartments. It needs a complete regeneration plan that would organically connect residential, commercial, and recreational spaces. Simply put, dilapidated housing in low-density areas should be incorporated into large-scale mixed-use development. Some of the city’s commercial and recreational needs should be moved underground. And all these should be seamlessly accessed through ingenious infrastructure and transportation planning.
In the meantime, the government had better expedite their negotiation with Washington for a quicker transfer of land within Yongsan Garrison, as promised well over three decades ago.
articles.summary: Even the historic Yongsan Park isn’t safe from the government’s desire for more housing.

articles.title: A Golden Chance to Protect the Pacific’s ‘Blue Corridors’
articles.full_text:
If Albanese is serious about a Pacific COP, he must heed the region’s call on oceans.
The next few months will see a flurry of climate diplomacy involving the Pacific Islands. Later this week, regional leaders are heading to Palau for the Pacific Islands Forum, with this year’s meeting expected to put ocean protection at the forefront. In early October, the world will travel to Fiji and Tuvalu for the pre-COP meeting; in November, Australia will preside over COP31 in Antalya, Turkiye.
Between now and then, Australia has a rare opportunity: to use its COP31 presidency and the new High Seas Treaty to help create connected protection across the Pacific and the high seas.
The idea behind this connection are the Blue Corridors, the migratory pathways used by whales, sharks and other marine species as they travel thousands of kilometers across multiple jurisdictions. To better protect these dynamic habitats, governments must connect networks of marine protected areas across borders and the high seas, while reducing the growing risks species face along their journey.
Consider the humpback whale. This month, humpbacks breeding off Queensland migrate toward Antarctic feeding grounds, while those in Tonga travel through the Cook Islands, Niue, and New Zealand to the same destination. To the whale, Australia, the Pacific Islands, and Antarctica are a single living system. 
Marine life depends on connectivity; protecting isolated marine parks is not enough. We must protect the pathways species travel.  
For years, this was impossible without an international law to protect waters beyond national jurisdiction. That changed in January, when the High Seas Treaty entered into force, enabling governments to protect the two-thirds of the ocean beyond any single nation’s control. Now, COP31 presents an opportunity to put oceans at the heart of the climate agenda, recognizing that the climate and ocean crises are inseparable.  
Science, law, and political leadership have aligned. Thirty years of migration tracking, complementing thousands of years of Indigenous knowledge, have revealed these ocean pathways, and governments now have the tools to protect them. Pacific nations are leading ocean conservation, consistently translating ambition into policy, diplomacy, and action.  
In May, Papua New Guinea, Fiji, and Vanuatu signed the Melanesian Ocean Corridor of Reserves, the first Pacific-led declaration linking national waters into a shared corridor of protection. Tonga has announced a National Ocean Policy with a vision for 30 percent protection and is signaling a further step: protecting the Pacific Blue Corridor that humpbacks travel, from Tongan breeding waters south through Cook Islands, Niue, and New Zealand toward Antarctic feeding grounds.  
This is the leadership nature demands, grounded in the millennia-old Pacific knowledge that the ocean is a pathway, not a barrier. The Blue Corridors concept shows how solutions can be locally led, informed by science and Indigenous knowledge, regionally connected, and globally scalable through the High Seas Treaty. Ancestral knowledge is reinforced by science and formalized in law, forming an essential foundation of ocean governance. 
What Pacific nations seek from Australia at COP31 is not endorsement, but enduring partnership, as demonstrated at the negotiating table in Antalya and in the decisions Australia makes before delegates arrive. 
Australia has framed COP31 as the Pacific COP, delivered in partnership with the region. Its role is to translate Pacific leadership into concrete outcomes through three key actions.
First, off Australia’s coast, the Lord Howe Rise is a submerged Tasman Sea plateau and biodiversity hotspot, straddling domestic waters and high seas. It’s home to many migratory species and ancient corals. Commitments to strengthen protections are a welcome first step toward securing its future. 
Second, Australia must strengthen protection in its own waters. The government has committed to expanding highly protected marine sanctuaries from 24 percent to 30 percent by 2030. Fulfilling this means firstly increasing protection in the Coral Sea, and around Lord Howe and Norfolk Islands, followed by further protections around the country guided by science.  
Third, marine sanctuaries alone cannot safeguard a rapidly warming ocean. Australia cannot credibly lead global climate negotiations while approving fossil fuel projects that accelerate ocean tipping points Pacific communities have warned about for years. Nearly 100 civil society organizations have already called on Australia and Turkiye to lead by example and “advance the just, orderly, and equitable transition away from fossil fuels.”  
The urgency is real. CSRIO modeling suggests that one of conservation’s great successes, the recovery of humpback whale populations, could be significantly reversed by 2050 as climate change disrupts Antarctic ecosystems. Decades of research have mapped the whales’ migration corridors, but a warming ocean is already reshaping the conditions that sustain these movements. 
A humpback breeding off Queensland follows the ocean, guided by forces older than any border. Her migration is based on instinct, but the future of her path will be shaped by human decisions. Protecting Blue Corridors means addressing the drivers of ocean decline, safeguarding critical habitats, and reducing threats along the journey of migratory species. 
The science is settled, the legal framework exists, and Pacific leadership is delivering. The decisions Australia takes before COP31, and the ambition it brings, will help determine whether Blue Corridors become this decade’s defining ocean achievement, or another opportunity that governments let slip.

articles.title: How an Election in Okinawa Will Impact East Asian Security
articles.full_text:
Incumbent Governor Denny Tamaki is known for his staunch anti-U.S. base sentiment. His re-election bid will ripple through the alliance and beyond.
Okinawa Prefecture will hold its gubernatorial election on September 13. Incumbent Governor Denny Tamaki, in office since 2018, is seeking a third term. His main challenger is Koja Genta, a former deputy mayor of Naha backed by the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). While local elections in Japan typically center on issues like the local economy and social welfare, Okinawa’s pivotal geographic location means this election could become a critical variable influencing the future security situation of East Asia.
Okinawa sits at the heart of the First Island Chain and is the Japanese territory closest to both Taiwan and mainland China. Consequently, since the end of World War II, Okinawa has served as the U.S. military’s “Keystone of the Pacific,” bearing a heavy military burden. Currently, nearly 70 percent of U.S. military bases in Japan are located in Okinawa. 
Beyond the U.S. presence, Japan’s Self-Defense Forces (SDF) are also expanding their deployments in Okinawa as the country accelerates a defense strategy known as the “Southwest Shift.” For instance, the Ground Self-Defense Force’s 15th Brigade, stationed in Okinawa, is set to be reorganized into a division by March 2027, increasing its personnel from 2,300 to 3,900. Furthermore, over the past decade, the Japanese government has deployed SDF units to Yonaguni, Miyako, and Ishigaki, islands located west of Okinawa Island, while bolstering radar, air defense, and rapid-response capabilities to counter the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) growing military activity in the East China Sea and the Western Pacific beyond the First Island Chain.
In fact, the PLA and the SDF have frequently engaged in standoffs in the area in recent years. On December 6, 2025, a fighter jet launched from a Chinese aircraft carrier locked radar on an Air Self-Defense Force fighter while flying over the high seas southeast of Okinawa Island, sparking a strong protest from Tokyo. Additionally, Chinese naval fleets and joint Chinese-Russian fleets have frequently transited the waters surrounding these islands. These developments underscore how Okinawa is increasingly becoming a frontline for great power confrontation.
For the people of Okinawa situated at the eye of the storm, the issue of U.S. and Japanese military deployments is not a simple matter of support versus opposition. It involves conflicting inner sentiments. 
On one hand, as China increases its activities near Okinawa – particularly with frequent patrols by its coast guard vessels in the waters around the Senkaku Islands (known in China as the Diaoyu Islands) – Okinawan perceptions of the military forces stationed there are shifting. According to public opinion polls, a greater number of Okinawans now view the presence of the SDF and even the U.S. military as necessary compared to the 1970s, shortly after the islands’ return to Japan. 
On the other hand, this shift does not alleviate Okinawans’ collective anxiety. For Tokyo, the deployment of missiles, radar systems, and SDF units may signify enhanced deterrence and situational awareness. However, for the local residents, these facilities also imply a higher likelihood that their home could become a frontline in a conflict or a target for attack. This has sparked a contradictory mindset and an enduring debate among the Okinawan people: Do military assets guarantee their safety or bring greater danger?

However, the LDP’s victory in all four of Okinawa’s electoral districts during the February 2026 House of Representatives election clearly served as a warning sign for Tamaki. Furthermore, a capsizing incident in March involving boats participating in protests against the Henoko base, which resulted in two fatalities, including a student on a school trip, triggered criticism directed at Tamaki, a staunch opponent of the base. The upcoming election will serve as a critical test of Tamaki’s stance against the Henoko base, the expansion of SDF deployments in Okinawa, and joint Japan-U.S. military exercises.
This is why the contest between Tamaki and Koja holds significance that extends beyond local politics. If Tamaki is re-elected, Tokyo may continue to face political resistance from the Okinawa prefectural government. While a governor cannot single-handedly halt the Japanese government’s national defense policies, a local government opposed to Tokyo’s military agenda can still raise the political costs of implementation and engage in ongoing bargaining regarding the burden of military bases and local interests. Conversely, a victory for Koja could present a significant political opportunity for Tokyo. However, if Tokyo can convince Okinawa that strengthening defenses serves not only Japan’s national security but also the protection of Okinawa itself, then the military deployment in the Nansei Islands might secure a more stable political foundation. However, this is clearly an outcome that neither Tokyo nor Washington desires.

articles.title: Taiwan: A Growing Economic Partner for the EU in Troubled Times
articles.full_text:
EU-Taiwan relations increasingly resemble a form of functional strategic partnership, despite the lack of formal diplomatic recognition.
Workers decorate with European flags ahead of the European Chamber of Commerce’s 2018 “Europe Day Dinner” in Taiwan, May, 17, 2018.
Much has changed since September 2021, when the European Union launched its Indo-Pacific strategy. In less than five years, armed conflicts in Ukraine and in the Middle East have shocked Europeans who know they can no longer fully rely on the close protection of their traditional ally, the United States. Although the U.S. remains NATO’s largest military power, Washington’s recent signs and messages have brought confusion to Europe. In some ways, East Asia faces a similar situation, where Japan and South Korea are now looking at diversification options.
Meanwhile, the EU is trying to “pivot” toward Asia, and has developed multiple ties with Japan, India, South Korea, and ASEAN. In that context, Taiwan remains a special case due to its unique situation as the world’s premier producer of high-end semiconductors. As Europe seeks to diversify supply chains and reduce vulnerabilities in strategically important sectors, Taiwan’s comparative advantages have become increasingly aligned with European interests.
Within this broader transformation, Taiwan has emerged as a significantly more important partner for the EU than at any previous point since diplomatic relations between the EU and the People’s Republic of China were established, 41 years ago. Once viewed primarily as a trading partner constrained by the EU’s adherence to the “One China” policy, Taiwan has increasingly been incorporated into European discussions on semiconductor resilience, critical technologies, cybersecurity, digital governance, and Indo-Pacific stability. 
In the past five years, Europe has become acutely aware of the importance of Taiwan. European delegations, from Brussels to EU member-states, have visited Taipei frequently; the number of engagements has surged by 20 percent since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the EU-Taiwan Tracker by CEIAS. Cooperation projects in technology and education have multiplied. The Taiwanese authorities have been welcoming and open to collaboration. 
In addition, the EU also started to engage with Taiwan through costly commitments. On December 1, 2025, Taiwan and the German manufacturer Merck announced a “Semiconductor Solutions Site” in Taiwan’s Kaohsiung city. Similarly, in July 2023, the ribbon was cut for ASML’s Linkou campus in Taoyuan city. This shows that while geopolitical uncertainty lies ahead, economic ties still manage to form. 
Despite the tricky waters both countries find themselves in, the numbers are clear: Taiwan’s Overseas Community Affairs Council (OCAC) announced that between 2016 and 2025, Taiwan investment in the EU amounted to US$13.88 billion, a 650 percent surge compared to just US$1.85 billion between 2006 and 2015.
As the EU is facing an increasingly challenging conversation with China over a trade deficit that reached 360 billion euro in 2025, Taiwan can stand out as a promising dialogue partner in the matters of technology and economic security. However, figuring out how to make the EU-Taiwan collaboration sustainable is more important than simply pouring in truckloads of investment.
While EU-Taiwan interaction is built on commercial activity, China has a long history of punishing any actor who shows the slightest friendliness toward Taiwan. Take the example of Japan: since a comment made by Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae in November 2025 suggesting that a Taiwan crisis might be a question of national survival for Japan, Beijing continuously slapped sanctions on Japanese companies. China added 20 Japanese firms to its export control list in February 2026, with another 20 added to the watchlist in June 2026. To use the Chinese axiom, Beijing is “killing the chicken to scare the monkey” – not only punishing Japan, but sending a warning to any country that might be tempted to follow suit. 
Takaichi has refused to back down. However, there is a major difference between the EU and Japan: the EU is not one single country, but a conglomerate of sovereign states. Whether the EU could handle such pressure by Beijing without scattering apart is not only under scrutiny by Taiwan but also a potential weakness to exploit for China. 
Although the EU will probably never become a conventional security actor in the Taiwan Strait, increasing concerns regarding economic coercion, supply chain disruption, cyber threats, and hybrid warfare have expanded opportunities for cooperation in non-traditional security domains and led to a shift in thinking. Consequently, EU-Taiwan relations increasingly resemble a form of functional strategic partnership, whereby cooperation develops through economic security, technological resilience, and institutional coordination, despite the lack of either formal diplomatic recognition or collective defense agreements.
As Europe is gearing up for multiple economic and technological conflicts in the months to come, Taiwan could become a promising partner for the EU in key areas. It is time for both the EU and Taiwan to use their respective strategic leverage and seize the opportunity. 
However, that is easier said than done. Not only is the EU divided by country, but attitudes toward China are also polarized in terms of party affiliation in each EU member state. Take Germany’s CDU/CSU-SDP coalition for example. While both governing parties support continued economic engagement with Beijing, their approaches differ. The SPD, with longstanding ties to trade unions and traditional industries heavily exposed to the Chinese market, places greater emphasis on balancing “de-risking efforts” with preserving commercial interests. By contrast, the CDU/CSU has adopted a stronger focus on industrial competitiveness, supply-chain resilience, and technological autonomy. Consequently, it has been more supportive of deeper semiconductor and high-tech cooperation with Taiwan, increasingly viewing Taiwan as a strategic partner in Germany’s economic-security agenda. This exposes another layer of complexity in terms of the heterogeneity of China-dependence on both inter- and intra- state levels.  
Hence, building on the above-mentioned observations, the issue is the underlying proposition of tying EU-Taiwan relations to EU-China relations. The argument here is that EU countries should pursue EU-Taiwan relations in parallel with EU-China relations, not subsequently. Taiwan, on the other hand, has sought to separate its cross-strait relations from its foreign policy since the Tsai Ing-wen presidency (2016-2024), emphasizing establishing international relations despite the cross-strait situation. However, this will only become effective if allies reciprocate the endeavor by showcasing support for Taiwan, disregarding the incrementally mounting pressure from Beijing. 
Taiwan has shown that the establishment of so-called non-red supply chains is possible, if one doesn’t lose the support of close allies. Economic deterrence is now even more effective than military and political coercion. The idea of resilience might vary by country, but for Taiwan, raising the cost of invasion for China could most effectively balance power asymmetry in the strait. With Chinese efforts to cut off Taiwanese international engagement rising and becoming more diverse and intricate, the EU should stand firm on its policy of competing on fair ground and not having to swim between two great powers during times of murky waters. 
While what lies ahead seems uncertain for the EU and Taiwan, one thing is for sure: a friend in need is a friend indeed.

articles.title: India’s Gen Z Protests: When Youth Rage Becomes a Beacon of Hope
articles.full_text:
India’s Gen Z protest undeniably reopened democratic spaces that had shrunk over the past decade.
Protesting students in New Delhi demanding the resignation of the Education Minister over exam paper leaks, July 2026.
Youth anger as reflected in Gen Z protests has set South Asia ablaze. Beginning in Sri Lanka and spreading to Bangladesh and Nepal, India is the most recent site of political upheaval caused by angry youngsters. 
Explanations for its causes and implications abound. In India, Gen Z protests erupted after a series of exam paper leaks and the formation of the Cockroach Janta Party, in reaction to disparaging remarks made by the chief justice of India about unemployed youth, calling them “cockroaches.” 
Some see the protests as a natural fallout of neo-liberal policies pursued recklessly since the 1990s, which created a chasm between enduring elite privileges and shrinking opportunities for youth amid growing inequality. Others invoke the usual “foreign hand” trope to support conspiracies to destabilize a strong regime. 
However, the intensity and spontaneity of the spread – cutting across caste and class lines despite a narrow agenda of plugging the paper leak and seeking the education minister’s resignation – took everyone by surprise. Geographically, it surpassed both the Jayaprakash Narayan-led movement of 1974-75 and the  2011-12 Anna Hazare-led protests, both also launched on anti-corruption planks.
Contrary to the Modi government’s expectations, the Cockroach Janata Party protest did not stay confined to Jantar Mantar, a designated site for protests in New Delhi that was its epicenter for 50 days. It spread across the country, including the northeast and southern states. 
The government’s usual playbook of branding protest voices as anti-national fell flat, and support for the movement swelled. Nearly a month into the protests, after the party’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke – he launched the party on Instagram – landed in Delhi from Boston and marched to Jantar Mantar, the government was forced into negotiations, resulting in the ouster of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. The minister’s resignation was the protestors’ demand from the beginning, one that they were unwilling to compromise on. 
The largely peaceful protest carried deep significance for the government and signaled important shifts in India’s political future. It exposed the rot in the education system and underlined the fading appeal of Prime Minister Narendra Modi among the youth, once his prime constituency. 
The recent statement from Mohan Bhagwat, chief of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (the mother organization of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party) that the protesters are not anti-national, and that protest is part of legitimate democratic processes, is a belated admission that the establishment misread the situation. 
This came as the Modi government found itself besieged from multiple sides, including a belligerent Parliament. The opposition sensed that Modi’s most difficult moment in his 12-year-old regime had arrived – his charisma fading, anti-incumbency rising, unemployment, inflation, corruption, and the Ram temple donation theft controversy in Ayodhya undercutting the government’s governance claims. 
Ironically, Modi’s rise to power was facilitated by the Anna Hazare-led anti-corruption movement of 2011-12, midwifed by WhatsApp, Twitter, and Facebook. Now, by a twist of fate, his regime is being undone on the same plank of corruption, this time through Instagram, the lifeline of the youth protest.
Every social movement has its own distinctiveness in framing agendas and creating a vocabulary of protest. Scholars like James Scott note that movements operate on two transcripts – public and hidden. The hidden transcript vents anger through coded satire, jokes, and humor against unresponsive regimes, and can be just as potent in undermining authority. The Gen Z protest made this evident, shattering Modi’s magic among youth through memes, parody, and mimicry – so effectively that he took to Instagram at midnight in an unsuccessful bid to recover lost ground on social media.
The protest’s impact continues to reverberate across India, and it is a bit too early to predict its trajectory. Unlike the 1968 French student protests, the Gen Z movement’s agenda is not radical; even its education reform demands are routine and administrative rather than comprehensive. If the movement’s implications are radical at all, they are chiefly psychological – the fear instilled by the state’s coercive apparatus has been overcome through protesters’ valiant acts.
Within the broader South Asian context, the Gen Z protests varied in character. In Sri Lanka, the target was the ruling party and its unpopular economic policies, aimed at toppling the government. In Bangladesh, the protest targeted authoritarian rule more than economic policy, ending in the restoration of a mainstream party. Nepal’s case differed: Gen Z succeeded in building a genuinely anti-establishment mood, though the subsequent government under Balen Shah has not pursued a radical or anti-neo-liberal program – despite neo-liberal policy being widely seen as the root cause of unemployment and inequality across these countries.
How should India’s Gen Z protest be assessed, and what does it mean for the country’s future? India’s demographic dividend – with half its population young – could become a liability if unemployment and human resource mismanagement aren’t addressed. This advantage is already being squandered, with unemployment soaring. 
An unmanaged reserve army of unemployed, skilled manpower could become an explosive force. A recent Azim Premji University report found nearly 40 percent of graduates aged 15-25, and 20 percent of those aged 25-29, are unemployed. 
No political dispensation holds a magic wand for this problem, as shown by the Gen Z protest’s eruption even in the state of Jharkhand, an opposition-ruled state. More disruption is likely as AI’s true impact begins to show. 
This is a wake-up call for the ruling party at the center, which bears the lion’s share of blame for mismanagement. Such a civilizational challenge at the human-technology interface cannot be addressed through slogans like Viksit Bharat (Developed India) or headline management. State freebies and sectarian divides may manufacture an electoral majority, but the lava of unrest will keep simmering.
There is a flip side to the movement as well. The fiascos of the Jayaprakash Narayan’s movement and Anna Hazare protests linger in public memory. The former wreaked havoc on university campuses without structural change in education; the latter belied hopes for political accountability and probity. People are therefore hedging their bets on the Gen Z movement’s outcomes.
Still, the Gen Z protest has undeniably reopened democratic spaces that had shrunk over the past decade. Streets have come alive again — a healthy sign for any democracy. 
Anton Jager, in “Hyper Politics: Extreme Politicisation Without Political Consequences,” argues that community formation for collective action is remote in the neo-liberal era; yet technology-driven digital community formation enabled collective action during this movement. 
It also bypassed left-right ideological distinctions and operated largely outside mainstream party frameworks — a pattern that could shape future political action. Whether Gen Z moves beyond social media content creation to effect radical, democratic change in this time of hopelessness and despair remains to be seen.

articles.title: What the Latest ‘2+2’ Dialogue Tells Us About China-Indonesia Relations
articles.full_text:
China wants more influence in Indonesia’s defense sector. Jakarta should make sure that also suits its national interests.
From left: Chinese Defense Minister Dong Jun, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, Indonesian Foreign Minister Sugiono and Indonesian Defense Minister Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin attend the 2026 2+2 Dialogue in Jakarta, Indonesia.
When Indonesia and China held their first “2+2” dialogue between foreign ministers and defense ministers in April 2025, the meeting marked a new chapter in the bilateral relations of the two countries. The two countries held the 2+2 dialogue again on August 21, 2026, in Jakarta. 
However, the significance of the 2+2 should not be measured solely by its symbolism. The strategic value actually lies in how far both countries can use the forum to manage differences while still maximizing their respective national interests. Already, this year’s 2+2 dialogue resulted in an agreement increasing the intensity of joint military exercises and plans to open joint munition factories in Indonesia, in line with the current national interests of both countries.
The relationship between Indonesia and China has fluctuated throughout history. Indonesia severed diplomatic relations with China entirely during the period from 1967 to 1990. Since ties were restored, the relationship between the two countries has continued to develop, and China has even become Indonesia’s largest trading partner. 
The closeness of the two countries in economic aspects influences the Indonesian public’s perception of China. According to “The State of Southeast Asia” survey released by the ISEAS Yusof Ishak Institute, if the geopolitical rivalry between the United States and China in the region were to escalate into an open conflict and Indonesia were faced with a scenario of having to choose sides, the majority of respondents from Indonesia would choose China. The preference for siding with China reached its highest point in the latest survey, at 80.1 percent.
However, China’s important economic position for Indonesia and even its clear “win” in survey results do not mean that Beijing can rest on its laurels.
China still has a lot of homework to do if it wants to secure its influence in Indonesia, especially when it comes to defense and security. When it comes to economic influence and public opinion, China significantly outperforms the United States – but in the defense sector, China is far behind. This lag is evident in both quantity and quality.
The data shows the gap in at least two aspects. First, the bilateral joint military exercises between the two countries. Based on IISS data, during the 2003-2022 period, Indonesia and China conducted joint exercises only four times. This number is far behind the 110 joint military exercises held between Indonesia and the United States during the same period.
Moreover, amid China’s emergence as one of the world’s top arms exporters, it can be said that Indonesia has not yet adopted Chinese weapons. According to data from the Laboratorium Indonesia 2045, throughout Indonesia’s history, its military has only operated three types of Chinese-made defense technology.
Both bilateral military exercises and the arms trade have long been believed to be instruments of defense diplomacy as well as strategies for exerting influence. And both metrics indicate that the defense cooperation ties between China and Indonesia are arguably weak. 
Beyond the statistical data as mentioned earlier, the defense cooperation between Indonesia and China is arguably weaker compared to that between Indonesia and the United States in terms of substance as well. The defense relationship between Indonesia and the United States appears to be more institutionalized, as shown most recently by the Major Defense Cooperation Agreement signed in April 2026.
Stronger relations are also evident from the resilience of cooperation between Indonesia and the United States. Although it experienced setbacks due to the imposition of an embargo and the suspension of Indonesian military officers’ participation in the International Military Education and Training (IMET), the defense relationship between the two countries was able to return to normal and continues to develop to this day. This is different from the China-Indonesia defense relationship, which is described as underdeveloped.
Considering the reality of the relatively weak defense relationship between Indonesia and China, the agreements reached in this year’s 2+2 dialogue will be important for both countries. The two key agreements are the commitment to increase the intensity of joint military exercises and the plan to build joint munition, rocket, and missile factories in Indonesia.
As previously mentioned, the intensity of military interactions between the two countries is still very minimal. China certainly does not want this situation to continue, especially in the context of geopolitical competition with the United States in Southeast Asia today. After all, Indonesia is often referred to as the natural leader of ASEAN. 
Increased joint military exercises will serve as an instrument for China to strengthen its defense relations and influence in Indonesia. The establishment of ammunition and rocket factories in Indonesia is certainly a strategy by China to increase the sale of Chinese weapon technology to Indonesia, which is still very limited. Moreover, Indonesia requires technology transfer in every purchase of arms technology from other countries. The joint factories would make it more tempting for Indonesia to acquire Chinese-made arms technology.
Meanwhile, for Indonesia, the increased intensity of joint military exercises with China can also be utilized as a form of strategic hedging. As a country that adheres to an “free and active” foreign policy, Indonesia does not want to be seen as being aligned with any particular power bloc. Therefore, Indonesia needs to ensure that its defense diplomacy with both the United States and China is equally strong. The establishment of joint munition, rocket, and missile factories can also provide alternative sources of new arms technology for Indonesia, which is actively modernizing its armaments. In particular, Indonesia is currently paying more attention to the utilization of missiles to implement an anti-access/area denial (A2/AD) strategy.
However, translating these agreements into mutual gain requires Jakarta to carefully manage accompanying strategic risks. Establishing joint munition, rocket, and missile factories with Beijing introduces complex challenges, including potential anxiety among ASEAN neighbors, technical friction regarding interoperability with Indonesia’s existing Western-heavy hardware, and scrutiny from Western defense partners. To maintain its non-aligned posture, Indonesia must ensure these joint ventures remain strictly focused on sovereign defense modernization and technology absorption, rather than creating strategic vulnerabilities or unintended geopolitical commitments. 
Ultimately, the China-Indonesia 2+2 dialogue reflects a convergence of pragmatic interests. For Beijing, it offers a key mechanism to deepen defense engagement in a vital region. For Jakarta, it provides a strategic opportunity to bolster their defense industry capacity and balance major power relations. If managed with strategic clarity and rigorous risk mitigation, the 2+2 dialogue can evolve into a pivotal mechanism for shaping regional stability and reinforcing Indonesia’s strategic autonomy.
When Indonesia and China held their first “2+2” dialogue between foreign ministers and defense ministers in April 2025, the meeting marked a new chapter in the bilateral relations of the two countries. The two countries held the 2+2 dialogue again on August 21, 2026, in Jakarta. 
However, the significance of the 2+2 should not be measured solely by its symbolism. The strategic value actually lies in how far both countries can use the forum to manage differences while still maximizing their respective national interests. articles.title: Pakistan Passes Legislation to Formalize New Military Command Structure
articles.full_text:
It operationalizes structural changes that have been unfolding within the armed forces over the past year.
Pakistan’s Chief of Army Staff General Syed Asim Munir visits troops participating in a field training exercise near Narowal and Sialkot, Dec. 3, 2024.
Pakistan’s National Assembly last week passed the Defense Forces of Pakistan Bill. The legislation is part of the ongoing broader set of reforms in the country’s senior military command structure.
The development is significant not merely as a procedural step but as a tangible move to operationalize structural changes that have been unfolding within the armed forces over the past year.
Defense Minister Khawaja Asif presented two related bills in the parliament, including the Defense Forces of Pakistan Act, 2026, and amendments to the National Command Authority Act, 2010.
Both bills had earlier been approved by the federal cabinet in a meeting chaired by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. A statement issued by the Prime Minister’s Office after that meeting described the bills as a continuation of the adjustments introduced under the 27th Constitutional Amendment. The Defense Forces Act, the statement noted, aims “to determine the relevant administrative matters regarding the office of the Chief of Defense Forces and the Chief of Defense Forces Headquarters.” Similarly, the amendments to the National Command Authority Act were described as a “necessary process” following the constitutional changes enacted last year.
The 27th Constitutional Amendment, passed by parliament in 2025, essentially altered Pakistan’s higher defense structure. It abolished the long-standing office of the chairman joint chiefs of staff committee and created the new position of chief of defense forces (CDF). Both posts are occupied by the chief of army staff. Moreover, Field Marshal Asim Munir became the country’s first chief of defense forces under the revised framework. Furthermore, the amendment also established the commander of the National Strategic Command (CNSC), which is a four-star office responsible for the operational integration of Pakistan’s strategic forces. These changes marked one of the most significant overhauls of the country’s top military hierarchy in decades.
The legislation approved last week carries those constitutional provisions into legal form and introduces further refinements. Arguably, the Defense Forces of Pakistan Act is designed to give practical effect to the CDF’s role as the overall commander of the armed forces. The draft of the bill explicitly states that the changes are intended to ensure “multidomain integration, restructuring and optimum jointness of the Armed Forces.” In essence, the provision seeks to reduce compartmentalization between the individual services and create a more unified operational posture across land, air, maritime and other domains.
According to the draft, the proposed legislation also enables the establishment of the Defense Forces Headquarters, which will serve as the central headquarters of the Armed Forces. This has ostensibly created a single institutional center under the CDF for coordination, planning and oversight that previously did not exist in the same consolidated form.
Moreover, the legislation has significantly expanded the formal authority of the CDF in relation to both the armed forces and the civilian government. Under the revised arrangement, the Defense Forces Headquarters will function under the CDF’s command. The CDF is now formally designated as the principal military advisor to the prime minister of Pakistan on issues of national security, defense, and all matters concerning the armed forces. Besides, the CDF has been granted operational command and control of the Armed Forces and has been made responsible to the federal government for matters of command and control.
The act further elaborates the CDF’s powers and functions, stating that the office-holder “shall exercise such powers and perform such functions as are necessary for multidomain integration, operational cohesion, coordination and oversight of all matters which have joint, tri-services and strategic implications for the Armed Forces and national security of Pakistan.”
In addition, the CDF now possesses authority to “retire, release, accept, or reject resignation of, or discharge from service, or retain in service, or relax age, or service limit of retirement” of personnel subject to the laws of the Armed Forces.
This authority, however, does not extend to those appointed under Article 243 of the constitution.
Article 243 of the Pakistani Constitution governs the highest-level military appointments, including the chief of naval staff, the chief of air staff, the chief of defense forces himself, and the commander of the National Strategic Command. These positions are filled by the president of Pakistan on the advice of the prime minister, so their tenure, retention, and removal largely stay under constitutional executive authority and beyond the CDF’s internal administrative purview.
The distinction seemingly preserves a formal layer of civilian oversight at the very apex of the military hierarchy even as operational and administrative authority is concentrated in the new CDF structure under these reforms.
Taken together, the bills represent another step in the institutional redesign of Pakistan’s armed forces.
The changes reflect an effort to modernize command arrangements and improve joint operational capacity in the aftermath of the 2025 conflict with India. Whether these changes produce the desired improvements in cohesion and effectiveness will eventually depend on how new reforms are implemented in the years ahead.
